News.title: Scientists 'stunned' by children's lung recovery in ultra low emission zone
News.content:
Scientists say they have been "stunned" by how quickly young children's lungs began to recover and grow after pollution restrictions were brought in where they lived.

Researchers found that children in London whose lung growth had been stunted by pollution showed impressive improvements after the introduction of an Ultra Low Emission Zone (Ulez) in 2019 reduced emissions.

The study followed more than 3,400 primary school children in London and Luton and provides what scientists believe is the strongest evidence yet that local clean air zones could help reduce some of the harm caused by pollution during childhood.

But independent researchers caution that other factors must also be considered.

Air pollution can stunt the growth of young children's lungs leaving them at an increased risk of asthma, heart disease, diabetes and even premature death.

Children are also more vulnerable to pollution because their lungs and immune systems are still developing. And when outside, they tend to be closer to the ground and nearer sources of exhaust fumes, for example.

In 2020 Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah, a nine-year-old girl from London who died following an asthma attack in 2013, became the first person in the UK to have air pollution listed as a cause of death.

In the study, researchers recruited six to nine-year-olds attending primary schools in London's ultra low emission zone and followed the same children for five years, comparing them to similar children (in terms of socio-economic background, physical activity and ethnicity) in Luton.

Children in the study had annual lung function and capacity tests in the year before Ulez came in and for four years after.

Initial results showed children's lungs in London were smaller in capacity than those in Luton, which is less polluted than London but has a similar mix of pollutants.

At the end of the study the children's lung capacity reached near identical levels in both groups.

"While we would expect children's lungs to grow year on year, our results indicate that the London children's lung growth had accelerated during the four years to 'catch up' with the control group in Luton to reach similar levels of lung capacity," researchers say.

"I was absolutely stunned when I first saw the results," Prof Chris Griffiths, a senior author on the study, at Queen Mary University of London, told the BBC.

"The speed of catch up in lung capacity in the London group was surprising and impressive.

"This shows an ambitious clean air zone can drive pollution levels down, rapidly restoring children's stunted lung growth."

The main test measured how much air a child could forcibly breathe out in one second after a big breath in.

In practical terms the improvements could mean children in the London group could run as fast as the Luton group without getting out of breath or blow out the same number of candles for example, Griffiths explained.

Another way of testing for lung capacity used in the study showed significant improvements too, though not to the same extent - implying there are still gains to be made.

Overall the proportion of children in London whose lung capacity was deemed "clinically impaired" (suggesting lung damage resulting in coughs or breathlessness) fell from 14% to 9%.

In Luton - where some smaller scale measures were put in place to tackle air pollution - the figures were 9% to 7%.

The team's measurements also showed the level of nitrogen dioxide children were exposed to fell faster in London than in Luton over this time.

Researchers say this is key as it likely demonstrates that the improved lung growth they saw was related to air quality improvements following the implementation of Ulez.

London's Ulez was first introduced in 2019 by Mayor Sadiq Khan in a bid to "clean up London's air". London had high levels of the harmful gas nitrogen dioxide which comes from motor vehicles.

Older, more polluting vehicles had to pay a daily charge to drive in central London. The measures were later expanded to cover the whole capital. While many supported the policy it provoked political opposition and protests.

News.title: Competition for degree apprenticeships quadruples as university costs rise
News.content:
Competition for degree apprenticeships in England has quadrupled over the past three years, the BBC has found.

The popularity of degree apprenticeships - which offer a paid-for university degree along with a salary - has grown as the cost of university has come under increased scrutiny.

Data seen by the BBC showed the number of applicants through the government's central platform nearly tripled from 8,100 to 21,800 over the past three years, while the number of positions available fell by almost half, from 7,300 to 3,700.

Applicants said they applied to university as a "backup" because competition was so fierce, with employers cutting back on hiring because of high employment costs and economic uncertainty.

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said it was "backing employers who take on young apprentices".

Last month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted to ensure teenagers had technical routes into careers that could rival the path of a traditional university degree.

His comments came as concerns grow about the immediate and long-term costs of university, with more students wanting to stay at home home rather than moving away, to save money and calls to reform student loan repayments. The cost of undergraduate tuition fees in England is now set to rise every year with inflation.

Degree apprenticeships might look to some like an attractive alternative, but the Freedom of Information data obtained by the BBC suggests they are hard to come by.

News.title: Camilla admits it was 'difficult' to keep King's cancer diagnosis a secret
News.content:
Queen Camilla has spoken for the first time about the pressure of keeping King Charles III's cancer diagnosis secret in the early stages of treatment.

In a video to mark the 30th anniversary of Maggie's cancer charity, the Queen, who is president of the charity, recalls how "difficult" it was to avoid discussing her husband's treatment while on an official engagement with cancer patients and their families.

In January 2024, the Queen opened a new Maggie's cancer support centre at the Royal Free Hospital in London.

She had just found out that the King had cancer and would need treatment but had to hold back from telling anyone as the official announcement had not been made public.

"Nobody could say anything at the time, that was quite difficult.

"I almost said something but, you know, I felt that it wasn't the time to say," the Queen told the chief executive of Maggie's, Dame Laura Lee.

"It was just a week before it became public and the courage that must have taken for you," Dame Laura told the Queen - referring to how personally challenging the hospital visit must have been.

"I was just longing to let it out, but obviously I couldn't," the Queen said.

The King's cancer diagnosis was revealed on 5 February 2024, just days after the Queen's engagement at the Royal Free Hospital.

More than two years later, he is still receiving cancer treatment. Buckingham Palace has reiterated that his health continues to move in a "positive direction".

In the seven-minute film recorded at Clarence House, the Queen says the King's way of coping has always been to push on with official duties. She spoke of helping to look after her "poor husband".

"Nothing stopped him. He just said, 'This is my way. I'm going to cope with it,'" she said.

During the visit, the Queen described feeling aware that she was now sharing the experience of so many families she met.

"I was almost questioning them. I didn't want to pry too deeply. But normally when I went in, I was just talking to them, but I don't know, I felt it was much more deep," the Queen said.

"I looked at everybody who was suffering and all the relations and I think it made me realise even more how important these places were."

The King has never disclosed the type of cancer he has, but has engaged widely with those treating and supporting cancer patients.

Maggie's says the King's public announcement prompted a 12% increase in men contacting them with a cancer diagnosis.

"The King's openness about his diagnosis has undoubtedly helped others to be more open themselves, and to now hear the Queen's completely understandable and natural response as a wife shines a light on why it is so important that family and friends also get the support they need," said Dame Laura.

"To hear her speak so powerfully of her own emotions when visiting the Royal Free centre, while knowing about his Majesty's diagnosis, is a huge honour."

Maggie's has 27 centres across the UK, built in the grounds of major NHS cancer hospitals, and supports hundreds of thousands of people each year.

News.title: Deaf patient given wrong jab due to sign language error, report says
News.content:
A deaf woman was given the wrong vaccine because she was not provided with a British Sign Language (BSL) interpreter at her doctor's surgery, a report says.

The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman (PHSO) said disabled people were being let down by inaccessible communications.

It said the patient, Samantha, had booked a flu jab but was instead given a Covid vaccine after staff failed to show her a BSL video which would have highlighted the error. She said the experience had had a "profound impact" on her.

The Department of Health and Social Care said the "deeply upsetting stories" were "completely unacceptable" and NHS and social care organisations had a duty to make services accessible.

The PHSO investigates complaints about UK government departments, public organisations and the NHS in England.

It said public services were legally required to support people with their accessible communication needs, which might be due to a disability, neurodivergence or English not being their first language.

Samantha had booked her flu and Covid jabs for separate weeks and showed a nurse a note on her phone which said she was there for the "flu jab only", the PHSO said.

Despite that, the practice said it believed it had correctly established Samantha wanted the Covid vaccine and had got her consent through her grandmother, even though she had early-stage dementia and was not in the treatment room.

Following an investigation, the PHSO recommended the surgery should apologise and pay Samantha Â£450. It has also since signed a contract with a sign language interpreting company.

The NHS Northamptonshire Integrated Care Board said it was "very sorry" about Samantha's experience, and that it expected practices to make "reasonable adjustments to support effective communication".

The PHSO said it had found disabled people risked not getting vital information about their healthcare, finances or employment because of a lack of accessible formats such as large print or audio materials.

Since April 2020, it said it had concluded 623 investigations related to reasonable adjustments, of which 496 were upheld or partly upheld.

The report also highlighted the case of Alan Graham, who was deaf and was being treated for heart failure at University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Trust.

When an interpreter was not available, hospital staff asked his teenage grandson to interpret for the family and tell Graham's deaf daughter that he might die.

News.title: First giant tuna caught off Yorkshire since 1960s
News.content:
Atlantic bluefin tuna have been caught off the coast of Yorkshire for the first time in an estimated 60 years.

The giant fish had not been seen in the North Sea since the 1960s due to overfishing and the depletion of herring shoals, according to researchers from the University of Exeter who have now tagged six off Whitby.

On Sunday, the five-person crew on board The Dominator landed a whopping 338kg specimen before repeating the feat a day later with a fish that weighed "just a little bit" less, according to crew member Jack Gardner.

"I have never caught anything like it," said the 28-year-old from the village of Paull, near Hull, describing it as the "best feeling ever".

Gardner, who has been on board The Dominator since 2018, said the crew had been about 10 miles (16km) from Whitby Harbour on Sunday when they made their first catch.

"It jumped out of the water, we all just looked at each other in awe," he said.

"We couldn't believe that we had actually hooked into one."

The crew had travelled to an area where they had heard the migratory species had been.

"Just as we were heading home we spotted a group of birds, so we went to try and have a look around there and that's when we hooked into one," said Gardner.

"We knew they were in the waters, it was just whether we could catch them or not because they are fast fish."

The crew dragged the fish for about five miles (8km) before they were able to get it aboard.

"The fight was a lot harder than I thought, the power of it," said Gardner.

Last year a 210kg bluefin tuna caught in waters on the south-wet coast fetched more than Â£2,000 at auction.

Gardner said the rare catch for his crew had already sold before the boat had arrived back in Whitby.

The following day they caught another bluefin tuna which also weighed more than 300kg.

The buyer, Lance Varrell from Hook to Plate, said the fish were "good quality" and would be sold on to restaurants, sushi markets and directly to customers.

"Bluefin tuna is very popular. It's a very premium fish - they call it the Rolls Royce of the sea," he added.

Itamaes (Japanese chefs) based in London would pay as much as Â£100 per kilo "if it's really good", he added.

Gardner said he was "immensely proud" of his crewmates Ben Shutt, Liam Crosby and their apprentice Ada, as well as skipper Clive Easton, for their role in the historic - and fruitful - catch.

News.title: Ovarian cancer and menopause at 19 mean I can't have kids, but it's changed me for the better
News.content:
Enlli started experiencing problems in 2024.

"My periods were changing, I was experiencing severe pain, but I was still being told I was fine," she said.

She described being "completely at a loss" and felt like she was "losing the plot".

But the pain became too much, and she visited A&E at Ysbyty Gwynedd in Bangor.

Scans revealed what was believed to be a cyst in her pelvic area, and she was placed on a medical plan to carefully monitor her condition, while continuing to work as a trainee mechanic.

"I was taking painkillers and working through the pain," Enlli said.

She then received a call from the hospital to return for further scans, and admitted: "My mind went straight to cancer."

Her worst fears were confirmed, and she was told she had stage 3 ovarian cancer, , externalwhich meant it had spread beyond the pelvis.

"Being told that I wouldn't be able to have my own children, I broke down and cried," she said.

"I had so much support, but it was so difficult hearing those words."

But Enlli said: "In a strange way I was kind of relieved when they told me I had cancer.

"Just because then I had an answer, I had a treatment plan, I was going to get better."

Enlli received fertility treatment, and seven of her eggs were frozen.

She finished chemotherapy in September 2025, and passed her driving test a week later.

Enlli now experiences hot flushes, brain fog, joint and muscle pain and fatigue, and says it can be hard to identify which are from the menopause or effects of the chemotherapy.

"My memory is absolutely awful," she said.

News.title: Suspended Reform UK member vows to fight to remain in party
News.content:
Political commentator Tim Montgomerie has told BBC Newsnight he will fight his suspension from Reform UK for criticising senior party figures in media interviews.

He said his appeal against suspension would be a test case of whether Reform could tolerate free speech.

The party said Montgomerie had been suspended in line with its rules after public criticism he made.

Montgomerie is a right-of-centre political commentator who defected from the Conservatives to Reform UK in 2024, and who has seen himself as a critical friend of the party leadership.

But it seems he is now regarded as more of a critic and less of a friend - and has had his party membership suspended.

On Friday, Montgomerie had told the BBC he was frustrated by party leader Nigel Farage's "aggrieved tone" after last week's Clacton by-election.

And on a Spectator podcast on Tuesday, he had said another senior party figure, Zia Yusuf, needed to become a team player and should not act "like a child" in politics.

It is understood his suspension came after the podcast was recorded but before it was released.

"I am going to fight this suspension. I want to stay in Reform. I didn't leave the Conservative Party lightly," he told Newsnight.

"I think Reform can reach parts of the country that the Conservative Party never will be able to so I'm going to fight my corner in Reform and I'm going to make this a test case of whether it is a party that can tolerate free speech and dissent," he added.

Montgomerie said he supported Reform's policies on immigration and welfare, but he has also highlighted internal tensions in the party.

In a video statement on X after news of his suspension emerged on the Guido Fawkes website, Montgomerie said he was only trying to make the party "better and stronger" with his public criticisms.

He added that Farage did not know about the decision to suspend him, and he had warned the Reform leader when he joined the party that he would be critical at times, as he had been of the Tory leadership when he ran the ConservativeHome website.

Reform's leadership will have to decide whether it is more politically difficult to rescind rather than to retain Montgomerie's party membership.

News.title: Burnham received £345,000 of donations ahead of becoming PM
News.content:
Andy Burnham has registered accepting Â£345,000 of donations over the past year including Â£164,347 from businessman Lord Sainsbury.

The donations, listed in the most recent version of the MPs' register of interests,, external are the prime minister's first declarations since he was elected to Parliament in June.

Separately, Burnham has also listed hospitality and gifts he received in the year before he returned to Parliament, including trips to Glastonbury, Lancashire Cricket Club and the Aintree Racecourse.

A Labour Party spokesperson said: "It's right that political campaigns are funded by the generous support of party donors, rather than via the public purse.

"All declarations have been made in line with Parliamentary and Electoral Commission rules."

New MPs are required to register all their current financial interests, and any registrable benefits (other than earnings) received in the 12 months before their election within one month of their election.

Lord Sainsbury's donations went towards Burnham's campaign to become Labour leader. Businessman Gary Lubner and former Greater Manchester night-time economy tsar Sacha Lord donated Â£25,000 and Â£35,000 to the campaign respectively.

The TV production company Charlie Parsons Creative contributed Â£50,000 and the think tank ThinkLabour, formerly known as Labour Together, provided Â£22,186.

The donations included the provision of office space, IT equipment, staffing, polling, travel, social media support and message testing.

Burnham's list also includes Â£20,000 of donations towards mayoral campaigning from the trade unions Unison, the Communications Workers Union and the Fire Brigades Union.

Labour peer Lord Blunkett appears on the list having donated Â£2,000 towards Burnham's campaign to become the MP for Makerfield.

Gifts and hospitality Burnham accepted when he was mayor of Greater Manchester include:

Four tickets to Glastonbury, where he was speaking at an event, from the festival organisers and Â£1,000 for accommodation from the campaigning group PRS for Music

Tickets worth Â£3,800 to the Brit Awards in Manchester from Sony Music Entertainment

Two tickets worth Â£500 for the Aintree Racecourse from the Jockey Club Racecourse

Two tickets, valued at Â£458, from Lancashire Cricket Club for a game in The Hundred tournament

A hamper basket and Wedgewood tea set worth Â£340 from the ambassador of Qatar

Shortly after becoming prime minister in 2024, Sir Keir Starmer became embroiled in a row over the gifts he had accepted including tickets to a Taylor Swift concert and thousands of pounds for clothes.

He subsequently paid back more than Â£6,000 worth of gifts and hospitality. He also tightened the rules so that serving ministers had to consider "the need to maintain the public's confidence in the standard of propriety" when accepting gifts.

News.title: Join EU migration pact to tackle small boats, says Ed Davey
News.content:
The UK should join the EU's new Migration and Asylum Pact as a way of tackling small boat crossings across the Channel, Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey has said.

The agreement, which came into force in June, aims to speed up the asylum process, increase the number of irregular migrants returned to their home countries and spread responsibility for asylum seekers across the EU.

Sir Ed argues that signing up to the pact would allow the UK to return asylum seekers to the first EU country they entered, thereby "destroying the business model" of the gangs behind the crossings.

Labour said the government's efforts to work with European countries to tackle small boat crossings were "bearing fruit".

A Labour spokesperson said more than 47,000 crossings had been prevented in two years and 70,000 people with no right to be in the UK had been removed.

"There's more to do and that will only happen by working in collaboration with the EU," the spokesperson added.

So far this year, more than 14,000 people have arrived in the UK by small boat - a fall of 43% compared to the previous year.

The EU's new pact, which was nearly 10 years in the making, introduces mandatory screening and an updated database to track those arriving in the bloc.

Under the rules, EU nations must take in migrants from those member states that see the highest number of arrivals - such as Italy and Greece - or instead provide extra funding or resources.

News.title: Mobile payments on the rise but cash decline slows
News.content:
Consumers are increasingly relying on their mobile phone to make payments rather than carrying bank cards, new data shows.

Two-thirds of adults in the UK were registered with at least one mobile payment service last year, according to an annual report by banking trade body UK Finance.

Use of a phone to pay has jumped in recent years. It is a decade since Apple Pay was launched in the UK.

While cash use continues to decline, the data suggests that the fall is slowing and that notes and coins will remain an important payment option for many people a decade from now.

Consumers are increasingly storing card details on phones or watches and making contactless payments backed up by facial or fingerprint verification, instead of pressing in a PIN.

Nine in 10 users of mobile wallets have their debit card loaded as their default payment method on their phone, with the remainder having registered their credit card.

News.title: Fire engulfs London waste centre
News.content:
A fire involving 50 tonnes of household waste has "severely damaged" a recycling facility in south-east London.

Fifteen fire engines were called to Landmann Way in South Bermondsey shortly before 20:00 BST on Monday.

London Fire Brigade (LFB) said the fire was brought under control just after 02:00 on Wednesday, with crews remaining on scene to extinguish pockets of fire.

The LFB said the cause of the fire was not yet known. Firefighters tackled a blaze at the same facility in June.

Speaking from the scene, station commander Duncan Rees said: "Crews worked hard in difficult conditions to bring the fire under control."

He added that ladders were used to tackle the flames from above.

News.title: British couple on honeymoon killed in helicopter crash on Greek island
News.content:
A young British couple and their pilot were killed in a helicopter crash on the Greek island of Sifnos on Monday, Greek police have said.

They have been named as newlyweds Alexander Cromie and Marie Ebert, who were in Greece on their honeymoon.

The private Bell 206 helicopter crashed just metres from a landing pad, killing the pair and their pilot, a Greek national.

The couple are said to have taken the helicopter from the village of Markopoulo near Athens to the popular holiday island, Kathimerini reported.

Greece's aviation safety authority told the BBC it was investigating the crash and that its investigators were heading to the scene on Tuesday to gather evidence and speak to witnesses.

Russian citizens are withdrawing billions of roubles from the country’s banks over fears that the Kremlin could seize deposits to fund the war in Ukraine.

Analysts say fears that the Kremlin could confiscate private savings to bankroll the conflict have triggered widespread panic, with more than 286.4bn roubles (£2.5bn) pulled from Russian banks during the first two weeks of August alone.

A staggering £5.3bn was reported to have been withdrawn in July on top of a further £3.32bn in June, according to Central Bank data.

Taras Skvortsov, an executive at state-owned Sberbank, has warned that total capital flight this year could be double of what was seen during the initial months of Russia’s 2022 invasion.

open image in gallery More than $3.4bn has been pulled out of the Russian banking system in the past two weeks

The cash run is creating a severe liquidity crisis for institutions already staggering under a mountain of bad loans— the result of Kremlin directives forcing banks to extend easy credit to military suppliers.

Skvortsov told The Washington Post: "Drones are flying. Things are burning down. Nervousness is growing.

"Everyday wisdom is kicking in. People feel they need cash under their pillow, not in banks where it may never be returned."

Such panic is not limited to ordinary depositors. Major corporations are frantically trying to shield assets beyond the reach of state regulators, routing capital through brokerage accounts in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Armenia to reach global markets.

The outflow has directly damaged state finances. With banks short on cash, the Finance Ministry was forced to cancel vital bond auctions intended to cover a budget deficit that has already ballooned past $76bn.

"Great powers don’t have repeated treasury bond failures in the middle of a war," Harvard scholar Craig Kennedy, told The Washington Post, describing the failure as a stark sign of "imperial overreach."

Fears have been heightened by Ukraine’s relentless drone campaign against Russian oil infrastructure, which has knocked out over 30 per cent of the nation's refining capacity and triggered a chaotic domestic fuel crisis.

open image in gallery Kyiv’s attacks continue to penetrate deeper into Russian mainland ( Reuters )

Meanwhile, high-profile asset seizures have convinced elites that no one is safe.

The state recently confiscated £5.6bn from agricultural tycoon Vadim Moshkovich, adding to the more than £36bn in private assets seized over the past year.

"If the government needs cash, Putin will just do a grab for assets," said an associate of one Russian billionaire. "He doesn’t care. And that’s where I think it’s heading."

The fiscal strain is now putting pressure on the state officials. Earlier this week, Andrei Klepach, chief economist at state bank VEB, was abruptly fired after he warned that Russia “could not win” a prolonged war of attrition against a Western-backed Ukraine.

open image in gallery Klepach indicated that escalating Russian military spending would be futile against a NATO-backed power ( Reuters )

“We’re under the illusion that everything [in Ukraine] will collapse. It hasn’t, and it won’t. Meanwhile, the costs we bear are mounting,” Klepach said.

The former economist’s words appear to ring true, with a widening budget deficit, collapsing bond sales, and record capital flight laying bare the immense financial toll of the conflict.

The message to the Kremlin from within its own establishment is clear: Russia cannot afford to keep escalating its military spending.

In an extraordinary intervention, Moscow’s powerful mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, issued a stark public warning against raiding from the civilian sector to fund the war effort.

"To kill the civilian economy," Sobyanin warned, "is to kill the country itself."

Archaeologists have discovered the strange remains of an individual placed deliberately at the bottom of a 2,000-year-old Scottish well, likely as part of an ancient ritual.

The Iron Age well, measuring about 3m (10ft) long and a metre (3ft) deep, was found lined with stone slabs and clay plugging gaps between them.

Researchers from the Highland Archaeology Services found artefacts near the well, which suggest it was built during the Iron Age, likely to hold water, long before it was abandoned and later used for ritual purposes.

The ancient well, according to archaeologists, is characterised by a “slabbed stone floor flanked by large foundation boulders and blocks, which were overlain by several regular horizontal stone courses and steep entrance steps”.

“The bonding of the lower levels of this structure with a viscous, clay-like mortar likely points to its function for holding liquid, and its use as a ritualised well has been suggested,” according to a report published by the Highland Archaeology Services.

Within the well’s internal area, there were several deposits, whose base was used to lay out an “adult human burial”, researchers wrote.

Human burial found in what may have been ritual well in Scotland ( Highland Archaeology Services )

A large quantity of animal bones were also found along with the buried human remains.

The human skeleton was capped by a “charcoal-rich material” that likely points to the well being abandoned, researchers say.

“The apparent blocking of the stepped staircase into the structure appeared to bear this theory out,” they wrote. A shale bangle fragment and a broken steatite bowl found near the well suggest they were from the Iron Age period. Such burials containing artefacts in northern Scotland are usually rare from the Iron Age period, archaeologists say.

Future analysis could confirm the sex and age of the human remains, they say. Researchers suspect the burial was likely part of a ritual conducted when the well was not in use for storing water.

It is located near another Iron Age settlement at Camore Wood, where the remains of at least 20 hut circles were previously found.

The newly discovered well burial may also be surrounded by hut circles, according to a report published earlier this month.

“Additional post-excavation analysis of the human skeleton, material culture, soil samples and ecofacts would add to the understanding of these features and, therefore, a range of further post-excavation analysis work was recommended,” researchers wrote.

Chinese comedy star Guo Degang is under investigation for allegedly changing the lyrics of a famous revolutionary song during a performance in Wuhan.

Guo altered a line in the Chinese song “Playing My Beloved Pipa” during a show on 24 July, replacing a reference to Weishan Lake with the Forbidden City, according to The Paper.

The Wuhan municipal bureau of culture and tourism opened an investigation on 11 August, saying the improvised section wasn’t included in the material submitted for approval. The performance itself was legally approved.

According to the bureau, the change was suspected of violating the Regulations on the Administration of Commercial Performances.

Guo, 53, is one of China’s best-known comedians and a leading figure in the revival of Xiangsheng or crosstalk, a traditional form of comic performance built around dialogue, wordplay, and storytelling.

He founded the Deyun Society, which helped bring the art form back to mainstream audiences and even took it to the international stage.

open image in gallery Guo Degang is under investigation for changing the lyrics of a famous revolutionary song during a performance in Wuhan ( Getty )

What sounds like a throwaway comic alteration by Guo carries significance in China, where the song occupies a distinctly patriotic place.

“Playing My Beloved Pipa” comes from the 1956 film Railway Guerrilla and celebrates communist guerrillas fighting Japanese forces during the Sino-Japanese war. In 2019, it was among 100 songs chosen by the ruling Communist Party’s publicity department to mark the 70th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China.

The original line describes the sun setting in the west before declaring that all is quiet on Weishan Lake. Guo instead sang that all was quiet in the Forbidden City. He even added comic lines like “I am Buddha, I am Tathagata, Mommy, Mommy, please”, and, according to the local outlet Sina, performed the song in a deliberately comic style.

The performance led to a complaint accusing Guo of having “not only distorted and vulgarised a classic revolutionary work, but also violated public morals and accepted standards of conduct”, CNN reported.

The Wuhan culture and tourism bureau confirmed that its investigation into Guo was still underway.

open image in gallery The Forbidden City remains one of the most powerful symbols of political rule in China ( AFP/Getty )

For almost 500 years, the Forbidden City, a vast palace complex in central Beijing, was home to emperors and the centre of imperial government, with the palace itself designed to embody the authority of the ruler. Although the monarchy ended over a century ago, the Forbidden City came to stay as one of the most powerful symbols of political rule in China.

That makes the altered lyric, in which the sun is setting in the west and the Forbidden City is “quiet”, more loaded than the original, fuelling speculation the line is a metaphor for the decline of political power.

However, authorities insisted their case against Guo was about the improvised section being absent from the material submitted for approval.

In China, commercial performances are subject to prior approval from cultural authorities, with organisers required to submit details of the programme and supporting audio or visual material.

Any change to the information submitted can require the performance to be approved all over again.

open image in gallery Guo Degang is one of China’s biggest comedy stars and a leading figure in the revival of Xiangsheng, or crosstalk, a traditional form of comic performance built around dialogue, wordplay, and storytelling ( Getty )

Guo had already found himself on the wrong side of China’s cultural gatekeepers once before. In 2010, one of his pupils assaulted a Beijing Television cameraman who had gone to Guo’s home to report on an alleged dispute over an extension to the property.

Guo attacked the media over the incident, drawing a response from the state broadcaster CCTV, which condemned the comedian without naming him and described the behaviour at the centre of the row as vulgar and ugly, according to China Daily.

The controversy came as the Communist Party was mounting its campaign against the so-called “three vulgarities”: yongsu, or vulgar culture; disu, meaning lowbrow or crude culture; and meisu, referring to culture pandering to popular tastes. Guo’s crosstalk, which often dealt with sex, corruption and social problems, became caught up in the campaign.

The fallout saw Deyun Society suspend its regular performances at four Beijing venues and carry out an internal “rectification”. Moreover, major Beijing shops removed Guo’s books and audio recordings while TV stations took programmes featuring him off air.

Guo’s case echoes the crackdown that followed a joke by stand-up comedian Li Haoshi in 2023. During a Beijing performance, Li compared his two dogs’ behaviour to a slogan used by president Xi Jinping to praise the People’s Liberation Army.

Beijing police opened an investigation into Li for allegedly insulting the army, while the city’s culture authorities fined his comedy company £1.4m, confiscated a further £148,000, and suspended it from performing indefinitely after finding that the material had violated regulations.

BBC presenter Emma Barnett has revealed that she had to undergo a hysterectomy that she “didn’t want to have” as a result of her crippling endometriosis.

The 41-year-oldToday programme host said her symptoms became “a lot worse” in her final weeks of filming documentary Fighting Endometriosis, in which she discusses her life-long struggle with the condition.

Just two days before the documentary aired in June, Ms Barnett had to undergo a sudden and extensive endometriosis surgery, a hysterectomy to remove her womb and a gallbladder removal.

She wrote on Substack: “I felt blind-sided and robbed. Even though my care had been superb and doctors, utterly brilliant.

“But this was not the road I had envisioned for myself. I had the hysterectomy I never wanted to have.”

open image in gallery Ms Barnett first revealed her diagnosis in 2024 ( BBC/Raw Media Productions )

Ms Barnett has frequently spoken out about the debilitating pain she experiences from endometriosis, a condition where tissue grows outside the uterus and causes swelling, bleeding, and severe pain during a period.

She said she did not want or plan to have her recent surgery, but said the situation became “urgent and non-negotiable”.

“I didn’t want this procedure because it’s major surgery. It’s frightening and a hard recovery - something I am living now. I didn’t want it because I wanted there to have been medicine or treatment to help my endometriosis. It felt and feels too extreme.

“Is such major surgery what anyone would ‘choose’? Yes, I officially and legally consented to the procedures - in so much as you can know what you are letting yourself in for.”

Ms Barnett said she did not “buy into the idea that the womb is sacred and at the heart of being a woman. I am still very much a woman and me.

“I am grateful to it because somehow it managed to help me have two children. Having your womb removed without having children if you wanted them is a totally different situation - one I must acknowledge.”

open image in gallery Endometriosis costs the UK economy £8.2bn a year ( Alamy/PA )

Earlier this year, Ms Barnett spoke out about a “horrific” experience with endometriosis where she couldn’t “remember a single thing” about a radio broadcast after being hit with intense pain.

The presenter previously had a laparoscopy, a surgical procedure to surgically remove endometriosis, which she said was difficult to recover from, and provided no pain relief.

She returned to air on Wednesday morning after an 11-week recovery, which she described as “one of the most humbling experiences of my life.”

The cause of endometriosis is unknown and affects around one in 10 women, according to Endometriosis UK.

Some 1.5 million women in Britain suffer from the condition, which costs the UK economy £8.2bn a year in treatment, loss of work and healthcare costs.

The civil war within Reform UK has intensified after a high-profile ally of Nigel Farage vowed to challenge his suspension to test whether the party can “tolerate free speech”.

Tim Montgomerie, a commentator and senior party figure, was suspended on Tuesday after he criticised home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf for not being a “team player”.

He has been openly critical of Mr Yusuf in recent weeks and even publicly suggested in a podcast that “Nigel has fallen out of love with Zia”.

open image in gallery Tim Montgomerie has vowed to make his suspension ‘test case’ ( BBC )

Mr Montgomerie told the BBC’s Newsnight programme that he is "going to fight" his suspension.

He said: "I think if that is the sort of censorship that the party wants to impose on me, that is not healthy.

"I'm gonna make this a test case of whether it is a party that can tolerate free speech and dissent."

He added: "I am going to fight this suspension. I want to stay in Reform. I believe that Reform's policies from immigration to crime to the ones that Robert Jenrick announced yesterday on welfare are the right ones for this country."

Earlier, in a statement on his suspension, he also claimed that Mr Farage had not known about it before it happened.

open image in gallery The civil war within Nigel Farage’s party has burst into the open

Last week Reform’s leader hit out at Mr Yusuf for calling a former Tory defence secretary, and soldier, Ben Wallace a “traitor”.

Speaking on The Spectator’s Coffee House Shots podcast earlier this week, Mr Montgomerie said of Mr Yusuf: “It was unprecedented for Farage to criticise him last week, but did he take down the tweet that Nigel criticised? No. He wouldn’t. He’s loyal to Nigel as he has to be if he wants to succeed him, but in terms of being able to really play as a team player...”

“He has consistently freelanced on Twitter, on, for example, accepting Conservative candidates, Suella Braverman and Robert Jenrick, even though he knew they were being wooed. But it was his way of trying to undermine that policy.”

Reform said its general secretary and chairman “have had months of complaints regarding Tim’s behaviour and conduct. They saw fit to take action and protect the party”.

A senior Reform source also said the party would “never engage the Tory briefing wars and toxicity that goes with them - the correct course of action has been taken. Disagreements should happen behind closed doors, not in the eye of the national media.”

The row within Reform has overshadowed what should be a good week for the party, after Mr Farage was returned to Parliament on Friday with victory in the Clacton by-election.

News.title: Best wine at Waitrose this summer, according to an expert
News.content:
When it comes to choosing top quality wine, supermarket shelves are nowadays one of the best places to look. Varied and expertly chosen, Waitrose Cellar stands among the best supermarket options, with bottles sourced from all over the world.

With such a vast selection, it can be overwhelming to know where to start. From soft rosé for sunny days, to robust reds and even the canned type, Waitrose Cellar’s wine selections are chock full of crowd pleasers and distinctive vinos for every occasion. To help you narrow down your choices, I spoke to wine expert and founder of the School of Booze Jane Peyton.

Waitrose cellar is also a great place to snap up deals on your favourite plonks, for example, right now you can get 25 per cent off when you buy six or more bottles on selected lines and save up to a quarter on sauvignon blancs from around the world.



White wine

( Waitrose )

“When I host tasting classes, I like to include this wine so I can ask the group to guess the grape,” says Jane Peyton. “They smell and taste the floral, herbaceous notes of elderflower, jasmine, and thyme, note the high acidity and suggest a New Zealand sauvignon blanc or English bacchus. They are invariably surprised when I reveal that the wine is made in Moldova from viorica, a white grape that originated in that country.”

Peyton adds: “At £9.50 this is a budget friendly introduction to the ancient wine making culture of Moldova.”

( Trius )

“One word - nectar! ,” says Peyton. “No other term can so accurately describe a dessert wine.”

“What makes Trius vidal even more special is that it’s an ice-wine, which means the sweetness comes from concentrated sugars that froze inside grapes on the vine in Ontario’s Niagara peninsula,” she explains. Expect apricot, peach, honey, and tropical fruit notes from the vidal blanc grape which is “sweet but it is also acidic so it’s not sickly”.

“It’s sublime with charcuterie and pungent cheese as a foil against saltiness,” Peyton adds.



Red wine

( Orovela )

“Fans of big chewy, full-bodied reds - here’s your wine,” Peyton says. “It is from Georgia, the world’s oldest wine making culture, and made of saperavi, the country’s most widely planted red grape. Hefty tannins and fresh acidity make it a match for barbecued food, hearty meat or mushroom dishes, and blue cheese.”

( Strofilia )

“Agiorgitiko, which translates as Saint George's grape, is the most widely planted red grape in Greece.” Peyton says that this is a great wine for those who like beaujolais and merlot, and are looking to try something new without spending too much.

“Expect cherries and other red berries, a medium body, fresh acidity and soft tannins,” she notes, while adding that it would work well with tomato-based pasta dishes, pizza, and moussaka.

Rosé wine

( Recato )

“I’m partial to Portuguese wine and am diligently working my way through the 250+ indigenous grape varieties,” Peyton says as she recommends a rosé from the country. “This rosé is made from a blend of touriga nacional, espadeiro, and vinhão and its tasting notes suggest a bowl of summer red fruits including raspberry and pomegranate. Its crisp acidity and gentle spritz will enliven the palate ready to eat oysters, grilled white fish, and feta salad.”

Sparkling

( Plumpton Estate )

The wine expert’s sparkling wine of choice from Waitrose cellar is “a small batch English sparkler made by the wine industry’s future superstars at Plumpton College, the UK’s Wine Centre of Excellence”. It’s made in the same way as champagne from a blend of East Sussex grown pinot meunier, chardonnay, pinot noir.

“This is just what I long for in a pink sparkling wine – ripe red fruit, rose petals, honey, and toasty brioche enlivened by fine bubbles,” Peyton says. “Start a meal with this as an aperitif and finish by matching it with dessert – Eton Mess or dark chocolate mousse. Heaven.”

The boss of National Lottery operator Allwyn UK is stepping down after a nearly three-year tenure leading a “long-overdue transformation”, the company has announced.

Andria Vidler will leave her role as chief executive next month following an agreement with UK chairman Justin King.

She will be replaced by Phil Walker on an interim basis from September 7, who joins from betting shop chain William Hill.

Ms Vidler said she decided it was the “right moment” to hand over to a new boss to drive growth following the completion of a major tech upgrade to the lottery.

She took the helm at Allywn’s UK business in October 2023, before the company took over from Camelot to run the lottery in early 2024.

The start of her tenure was dogged by legal issues involving the Gambling Commission’s decision to award Allwyn the 10-year licence, which caused delays to its switch to a new technology provider but were found to be outside Allywn’s control.

It also delayed plans for new draw-based games and held back the amount of money the National Lottery can give to good causes in the early part of the licence.

This year, Allywn completed the lengthy £450 million major tech upgrade to the lottery, which involved moving 18 million player records and more than three billion historical transactions from old platforms to new ones, updating the lottery website and mobile apps, as well as transforming the technology used by retail partners.

It also paved the way for the group to unveil the biggest overhaul to its draw-based Lotto game since its launch in 1994 and the first new draw-based game in the National Lottery’s history this summer, with the launch of the UK-specific version of the world’s biggest jackpot game, Powerball.

The company said Mr Walker’s appointment will help drive forward a new phase of growth for the business while it searches for a permanent successor.

Mr Walker spent six years at William Hill in roles including its chief commercial officer and managing director for the UK and Ireland.

Ms Vidler said: “It has been a huge privilege to lead Allwyn UK through such an important period for the National Lottery.

“The last three years have required enormous focus and commitment from colleagues right across the business, and I am proud of what we have delivered together.

“But transforming the National Lottery is a marathon, not a sprint, and with the major transition now complete, and the National Lottery in a stronger position to keep delivering for the nation, this feels like the right moment for me to pass on the baton.”

Chairman Mr King said: “Since Andria joined us, she has led from the front through an intense period of change, helping to complete the much-needed and long-overdue transformation of the National Lottery.

“With the major transition milestones delivered, now is the right time to look to the future and build on the solid foundations that have been laid to create a strong platform for future growth.

“We are pleased to welcome Phil as interim CEO as we continue to modernise and strengthen the National Lottery for players, retailers and good causes.”

Regulated train fares in England could increase by more than 4 per cent next year, meaning season tickets will increase by thousands of pounds.

The potential rise is based on the Office for National Statistics announcing that Retail Prices Index (RPI) inflation rose to 3.2 per cent in July.

The Government has not confirmed what it will do about fare rises in 2027, but last year’s 4.6 per cent cap was one percentage point above RPI in July 2024.

If that formula is used to set next year’s increase, the cost of train travel will jump by 4.2 per cent.

That would mean an annual season ticket from Brighton to London rising by £219 to £5,423.

A flexi ticket for travel two days per week over a year from Leeds to Manchester would increase by £151.35 to £3,754.95.

The Government has not confirmed what it will do about fare rises in 2027, but last year’s 4.6 per cent cap was one percentage point above RPI in July 2024 ( PA Archive )

Sir Keir Starmer’s government froze regulated fares this year.

Based on the potential ticket price increases, we looked at 10 examples of possible rail fare rises in England.

Figures are based on an increase of 4.2 per cent. The table compares the cost of season tickets using any valid route bought before and after such a rise.

It does not include the price paid if within-London travelcards are purchased for Tube and bus journeys in the capital.

Annual season tickets

About 45 per cent of fares on Britain’s railways are regulated by the Westminster, Scottish and Welsh governments.

They include season tickets on most commuter journeys, some off-peak return tickets on long-distance routes, and flexible tickets for travel around major cities.

Unregulated fares are set by operators, but rises in these are expected to be similar.

Flexi tickets for travel two days per week over a year

What has the Department for Transport said on the potential ticket price rises?

A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “We are working to make transport affordable for everyone.

“The rail fares freeze is giving millions of people breathing space on their travel costs and is expected to save passengers on some of the busiest routes more than £300 a year.

“No decision has been made on fares after the freeze ends, and we are looking at all options carefully.”

News.title: Unemployment rate fails to fall for Burnham
News.content:
An expected drop in the unemployment rate has failed to materialise, dealing a setback to Andy Burnham’s hopes of reviving Britain’s ailing economy.

Unemployment remained stuck at 4.9pc in the three months to June, while the number of payrolled employees fell by 13,000, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics. Economists had predicted that the unemployment rate would ease to 4.8pc.

While the three-month figure was flat, monthly data showed a sharp increase at the end of the period. Unemployment jumped to 5.4pc in June, up from 4.6pc the previous month.

That marked the highest reading since October 2020 and the biggest monthly jump in 13 years.

Julian Jessop, at the Institute of Economic Affairs, described the latest jobs figures as “dire”.

He said: “The unemployment rate remains stubbornly high, with a big jump in the single month figure for June.”

It came as private sector wage growth slumped to a six-year low of just 2.8pc. That stands in contrast to a 6.1pc pay increase for the average public sector worker in the same period.

Meanwhile, vacancies dropped to 707,000 in the three months to July – the lowest level since 2021 – with a particular strain on entry-level job openings.

Ben Harrison, director of the Work Foundation at Lancaster University, warned that the UK was “trapped in a deepening jobs drought”.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said: “Stagnant, or even negative, real wage growth in the second half of this year will intensify the pressure on Burnham and Healey to come up with a package to support the cost of living.

“However, doing anything substantial without breaching either the fiscal rules or the manifesto commitments looks increasingly difficult given the deterioration in headroom and commitments to spend big on everything from defence to social care.”

News.title: Top British scientist steps down from WHO
News.content:
One of Britain’s best-known scientists has resigned as assistant director-general of the World Health Organization.

Sir Jeremy Farrar became a household name during the pandemic when he served on the UK’s Scientific Advisory Group for Emergencies (Sage).

Sources inside the WHO and the broader scientific community told The Telegraph he resigned his position on Monday.

While it is not clear what prompted his resignation, colleagues told The Telegraph he had been unhappy within the organisation for some time. One speculated that he had become increasingly frustrated with its internal politics and bureaucracy.

Sir Jeremy, 64, who was also a former director of the Wellcome Trust, could not immediately be reached for comment.

The surprise move comes at a difficult time for the WHO, which is undergoing a major restructuring after suffering cuts and a massive funding shortfall following the United States’s withdrawal from it in January. It is also fighting a major outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO’s Director-General, announced Dr Farrar’s decision in an email to all staff on Tuesday morning, saying that the British scientist will “retire” from the WHO, effective September 30.

In the email, seen by The Telegraph, Dr Tedros said: “Dr Farrar has demonstrated an exceptional commitment to science and public health at the highest levels, and we are grateful that he chose to bring his experience, energy and conviction to WHO.

“On behalf of the entire organisation, I extend my sincere thanks to Dr Farrar... [and wish] him every success in his next chapter and a well-deserved retirement.”

He added that Dr Bruce Aylward will take over as the new Assistant Director-General for Health Promotion, Disease Prevention and Care.

News.title: Rabies deaths are rising. What is going wrong?
News.content:
In a packed intensive care ward in Dhaka, three-year-old Abdul lay paralysed, his tiny body contorted by a rabies infection that had reached his brain.

His mother, Sheuli Akter, 38, sat at his side massaging his legs in the hope that this might loosen his muscles, but it was having no effect. Even his hands and feet were seized up by cramps.

Abdul had been in the hospital for a month but doctors said he was unlikely to live much longer. The infection, they said, had progressed to degenerative encephalitis; the virus had got to his brain.

Abdul was shaking, gripped by fever. His breathing was rapid and panicked, punctuated occasionally by groans of pain.

On his chin was the telltale scar of a dog bite, the source of the infection.

“He was playing outside with the other children,” said Sheuli. “The dog, which was one of those always waiting around outside, suddenly attacked him. They said it went for him because he was the smallest.”

News.title: Arsenal hunger is ominous for rivals as they dismantle Man City
News.content:
Was it the early goal that should have put Arsenal’s rivals on red alert? No. While Ricardo Calafiori’s intervention was dramatic, it wasn’t that. Was it the seamless introduction of the new signings, then? No, it wasn’t that either, despite the excellence of Bruno Guimarães and Christos Tzolis.

How about the emphatic scoreline – surely that was it? Again, the answer is no. Three unanswered goals against Manchester City will always grab a headline, but scorelines do not always define the nature of a performance or a team’s capabilities.

So what was it that should have those with pretensions of ripping Arsenal’s crown from their grasp shuffling uncomfortably? One word: hunger. The reason this was such an ominous afternoon for the chasing pack is the fact Mikel Arteta’s team played with intensity of a team with everything to prove.

Title wins can sometimes sate ambition. Players don’t always want to climb the same mountain again, not least if reaching the peak was initially so draining, but everywhere you looked on a day when Cardiff was painted red and white was evidence that Arsenal remain ravenous for success.

First Guimarães pounced out of the shadows to mug Jérémy Doku, leaving him in a heap. Then there was Gabriel Magalhães thundering into a befuddled Doku, celebrating in front of City’s fans as if he had scored, before Ben White flung himself in front of the Belgian, denying a clear-cut scoring opportunity.

News.content:

Bruno Fernandes missed a penalty for the second successive pre-season friendly as Manchester United were beaten 4-2 by former head coach Ruben Amorim’s AC Milan.

Fernandes did at least get an assist, taking the second-minute corner which was powerfully headed home by Harry Maguire to give United the lead.

Sports.title: Inside breakdown of Todd Boehly and Behdad Eghbali’s relationship with feuding Chelsea chiefs set to finally split

BLUE FAIL Inside breakdown of Todd Boehly and Behdad Eghbali’s relationship with feuding Chelsea chiefs set to finally split

THE marriage of convenience between Chelsea’s owners has been on the rocks for two years.

Now it is set to end in divorce over the coming months.



Todd Boehly and Behdad Eghbali have separate executive boxes at Stamford Bridge and have been living mostly separate lives for some time.

The billionaires have muddled on, keeping things civil for the sake of the children.

The terms of their relationship mean chairman Boehly and majority owners Clearlake Capital have to sign off on the day-to-day decisions governing life in the Blues’ dysfunctional family.

But they want different things and feel the time is approaching to go their separate ways.

The US authorities’ probe into Boehly’s friend and business partner Mark Walter is acting as something of a catalyst towards a permanent separation.

Both Walter and Boehly control 12.8 per cent of Chelsea via BlueCo22 Holdings. Swiss billionaire Hansjorg Wyss has a smaller stake.

As regulators and prosecutors investigate his use of loans from his insurance companies to fund other assets, Walter agreed to sell control of the Los Angeles Lakers.

But Walter and his companies deny all wrongdoing and say they are confident of a favourable outcome.

Boehly is under no such pressure.

All the money he puts into Chelsea and his other sporting ventures is his own.

He has held on-off talks with Clearlake Capital over buying each other’s shares since a big falling out at the start of the 2024-25 season.

Things will come to a head next summer when the arrangement for Boehly to be chairman comes to an end.

Next May will mark five years since the BlueCo consortium came together to take advantage of the forced sale of Chelsea.



Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich was sanctioned by the UK Government over his links to Russian president Vladimir Putin following the start of the war with Ukraine.

Having worked on deals with Clearlake before, Boehly had experience of success as co-owner of the LA Dodgers with Walter, as well as in other sporting investments.

Clearlake, co-founded by Eghbali and Jose Feliciano, are majority owners of BlueCo, holding around 61.85 per cent of shares.

Boehly was made chairman, on the understanding Clearlake would assume the role after five years, but quickly became the public face of BlueCo.



With his baseball cap and ideas like a North v South all-star Premier League game, it did not take long to make a name for himself.

Boehly was also interim sporting director for the first few months of the new regime, as Chelsea began a transfer spending spree which now stands at more than £1.5 billion.

But all big decisions — including player deals — were and are agreed jointly, with each “side” having a veto to block anything.

Although the club was routinely referred to as “Boehly’s Chelsea” for some time, the reality is Eghbali has overseen day-to-day operations since early 2023.

Some critics even accuse Eghbali of micro-managing Chelsea — claims his camp deny.



Others say Boehly has interfered unhelpfully, both while sporting director and even after taking more of a back seat.

The decision to axe boss Mauricio Pochettino after the 2023-24 season caused ructions.

Eghbali and his football executive team led by co-sporting directors Paul Winstanley and Laurence Stewart wanted Pochettino to go, despite an improvement on Chelsea’s chaotic 2022-23 campaign.



They believed Boehly reluctantly agreed, only for the club chairman to take Pochettino out for an end-of-season dinner which seemed like a vote of confidence.

But by September 2024, differences in opinion about how to run Chelsea came to a head.

The relationship between Boehly and Eghbali was said to be broken beyond repair.

Divisions also emerged over longer-term strategy, such as how to give Chelsea a 60,000-seater multipurpose stadium to generate the revenue to compete with European rivals.

Both the Boehly camp and Clearlake were bullish, briefing their confidence they could raise the money to buy out the other side.



Yet nothing happened.

The 2024-25 season under new boss Enzo Maresca was the most successful of the BlueCo regime.

Chelsea won the Conference League, earned a return to the Champions League and claimed the first edition of the revamped Club World Cup in the USA.



It is always easier to get on when things are going well.

And Chelsea reverted to type in 2025-26. Maresca left under a cloud in January amid links to the Manchester City job which proved well founded.

The Blues made the calamitous decision to bring in the inexperienced Liam Rosenior from sister club Strasbourg.

They spent yet another season without a long-term shirt sponsorship deal and without making any apparent progress on the stadium.

Whether Chelsea find a way to become part of the Earls Court redevelopment, come up with another new site or even revisit a revamp of Stamford Bridge, the likely cost is £5bn.



Neither side appears willing to put in their share of that massive outlay while the other camp has a significant say over the project.

Xabi Alonso, the SIXTH permanent boss under BlueCo, may put things on an even keel.

But there is no papering over the cracks in the boardroom.

As someone with knowledge of the situation observed, something has got to give.



At the end of May, Boehly is due to hand over the Chelsea chairmanship to Clearlake.

It would be the natural time for one side or other to put up or shut up.

Outsiders have always regarded Clearlake and Eghbali as more likely to take full control.

Buying the 25.4 per cent of BlueCo which Walter and Boehly own between them would give Clearlake over 87 per cent of the shares.

It would also end the veto system — although it is unclear how much either side has used it, if at all.



Reaching a deal will not be easy.

Both sides have to agree on a valuation of Chelsea and Strasbourg.

Neither side will give up custody of the kids cheaply but a split now feels inevitable.

Rashford has also been reunited with close friend Youri Tielemans, with whom he struck up a bond during his stint at Aston Villa. Former United skipper Harry Maguire has also thrown his weight behind Rashford staying at the club beyond the summer transfer window.

View 3 Images Rashford has been lending his experience to United's young stars (Image: Ash Donelon, Manchester United via Getty Images)

He recently said: "He's a huge threat to have in your team, if he's going to stay with us. Obviously the transfer window is still open, but we hope as players that he stays and he's a big asset to have.

‌



"I've played with Marcus for numerous years and I know that from playing against him, and playing with him in training, he is going to help us."

Last season, Rashford's standout displays earned him a spot in Thomas Tuchel's England squad for the recent World Cup. During his time at the Camp Nou, he racked up an impressive 14 goals and 14 assists across 49 appearances.

View 3 Images Rashford has been all smiles since he started training with United again (Image: Ash Donelon, Manchester United via Getty Images)

‌



His efforts played a pivotal role in clinching La Liga, marking the first league title of his footballing career. It is claimed that the prospect of a permanent move to Barcelona this summer remains very much alive.

TEAMtalk recently reported Barcelona's hierarchy remain in contact with Rashford's representatives, despite having already brought in Karim Adeyemi and Anthony Gordon this summer. United kick off their Premier League campaign this Saturday with a trip to newly promoted Hull City.

Sports.title: BBC brutally axes six Match of the Day pundits and confirms replacements
Sports.content:
BBC brutally axes six Match of the Day pundits and confirms replacements

The new Match of the Day line-up for the 2026/27 Premier League has been confirmed with a total of 10 changes to the rotating cast of pundits

Match of the Day: Nedum Onuoha and Stephen Warnock praise Brian Madjo

The BBC has scrapped six pundits from their Match of the Day line-up and added four others ahead of the 2026/27 Premier League season. Those not selected for this year include Martin Keown, Dion Dublin, Shay Given, Stephen Warnock, Nedum Onuoha and Theo Walcott.

‌



Keown leaves his position on MOTD after almost 20 years in the job, first joining the crew in 2007. Dublin also exits following a longstanding career on the programme, joining as a regular analyst in 2012 and becoming a familiar face.

‌



Given arrived in the studio in 2018, while Warnock joined two years later with Onuoha. Meanwhile, Walcott only started appearing on the show in 2024. Mark Chapman, Kelly Cates and Gabby Logan will retain their place as the main faces of MOTD.

‌



Four new stars have joined as replacements of the six departing. Ashley Young, Robbie Keane, Toby Alderweireld and Thomas Frank are all now part of the revolving door of guests.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Kelly Cates makes thoughts clear on Gabby Logan and Mark Chapman as she opens up on BBC job READ MORE :

Mark Chapman's BBC colleagues have all told World Cup host exactly what they think of him READ MORE :

View 3 Images Match of the Day will have new faces this season (Image: BBC)

‌



Fans will be relieved to hear that familiar faces like Alan Shearer and Wayne Rooney are returning to the show. Joe Hart, Micah Richards, Ellen White, Steph Houghton, Danny Murphy and Ashley Williams will also still be part of MOTD for the new season.

This announcement comes after The Sun claimed that a number of MOTD pundits were considering leaving to join Gary Lineker's new Netflix show, The Rest is Football. BBC regulars Richards and Shearer were often on Lineker's programme during the World Cup, dividing their time between the two.

The report also alleges that there were disagreements between unnamed MOTD pundits and BBC head of sport Alex Kay-Jelski.

‌



View 3 Images Frank has joined the MOTD team (Image: Sebastian Frej/MB Media, Getty Images)

Make it easier than ever to turn a regular fixture into something genuinely unforgettable.

However, the broadcaster rubbished these claims in an official statement, saying: "We have repeatedly told The Sun these anonymous claims are untrue and we look forward to bringing audiences the return of Match of the Day this weekend with its established line-up of presenters and pundits – alongside a host of new guest voices bringing fresh insight from inside the game."

‌



Alongside these new changes, the BBC will launch a new fan-forward show which will represent every Premier League side. 20 fans will collaborate on this programme which will be shared on the BBC Sport app's Shorts feed as well as the BBC Football YouTube channel.

The broadcaster states that this fan collective will "put supporters at the heart of the football conversation." Kay-Jelski has commented on their coverage, stating that fans will be put "at the heart" of their programming.

View 3 Images Shearer and Rooney will return to MOTD (Image: BBC)

He said: "Football means something different to every fan, and this season BBC Sport is putting those fans even more firmly at the heart of the game.

"We're bringing together the unrivalled expertise of former players and managers with the passion, personality and perspectives of supporters themselves to create a richer football experience wherever and however audiences follow the game.

"There are new shows, new voices and new ways to get closer to the action – alongside the trusted coverage millions of fans already turn to, from Match of the Day to BBC Radio 5 Live. Whether you want the big debate, the inside story, the fan perspective or simply every goal, BBC Sport will be there all season."

Sports.title: Everton chief drops fresh hint over Jack Grealish return - ‘We’ve remained in contact’
Sports.content:
Everton chief drops fresh hint over Jack Grealish return - ‘We’ve remained in contact’

Jack Grealish spent last season on loan with Everton from Manchester City albeit saw his spell on Merseyside cruelly cut short by injury and his future still remains up in the air

View 2 Images Jack Grealish has now returned to Manchester City (Image: Getty Images)

Jack Grealish remains ‘in contact’ with Everton as he attempts to clarify his Manchester City future. The England international spent last season on loan with the Toffees in an attempt to relaunch his career.

‌



Grealish, 30, enjoyed a bright start to life on Merseyside, scoring twice and providing six assists in 22 appearances before seeing his loan spell cruelly cut short by a long-term injury.

‌



He opted to stay with Everton throughout his recovery and the club’s CEO Angus Kinnear has since revealed that conversations remain ongoing with the winger, albeit stopped short of confirming whether he would be rejoining the club.

‌



"Jack [Grealish] is a player we've remained in contact with," Kinnear told BBC Radio Merseyside. "It was no secret that he decided to have his rehabilitation done here for the remainder of last season when he didn't have to do that.

"He's a player who's fallen in love with the right shade of blue but ultimately he's a Manchester City player at the moment and we need to respect that.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



"The most important thing is he's back. He had a very serious injury, he's worked really hard to get back from that."

Grealish has already made one appearance for Man City this season, having been introduced at the break of the Community Shield defeat to Arsenal.

Speaking about the winger, new City boss Enzo Maresca said: "Jack was inside when we were 2-0 down so the game already became complicated after that, but overall I think Jack was good.

‌



“The ones that are still here and want to work every day and if they deserve they're going to get minutes. At the moment the transfer window is open and we will see what happens."

View 2 Images Grealish enjoyed a productive spell at Everton before injury (Image: Getty Images)

Grealish joined City from boyhood club Aston Villa back in 2021 for £100m and has gone on to make 158 appearances, albeit has scored just 17 times. He has however helped the club to three Premier League titles, the Champions League and the FA Cup. Grealish’s current deal with City is set to run until next summer.

‌



The 39-time England international caused a bit of a stir over recent days, having been spotted at Cardiff City’s Championship opener against Wrexham, albeit there is no suggestion that he could sign for either of the two sides.

He was however asked by one of the home supporters whether his appearance was a permanent deal or a loan, with Grealish jokingly replying that he didn’t know yet.

He will hope to be in contention this weekend as Man City kick off their Premier League season against Bournemouth at the Etihad Stadium.

Sports.title: Harry Kane praised for Jamal Musiala reaction as star reveals 'neurological dysfunction'
Sports.content:
Harry Kane praised for Jamal Musiala reaction as star reveals 'neurological dysfunction'

Bayern Munich star Jamal Musiala collapsed for the second game running during Tuesday's friendly against Heidenheim, later revealing that he's been diagnosed with treatable absence seizures

View 3 Images Harry Kane gestured for players to form a shield

Harry Kane has been praised for his quick thinking after Bayern Munich team-mate Jamal Musiala collapsed mid-game for the second time in four days. Musiala, 23, dropped to the turf just eight minutes after coming on as a substitute during Bayern's 4-2 win away to Heidenheim on Tuesday in a pre-season friendly.

‌



England captain Kane spotted Musiala going down and quickly gestured for both sets of player to come over, urging them to form a shield the midfielder. Medical staff ran onto the pitch to treat Musiala, who was thankfully able to stand up and walk off under his own steam.

‌



On social media, fans hailed Kane for his compassionate actions. "Expect nothing less from Harry, classy," one user posted on X. "Kane is class on and off the field," another added.

‌



There was a similarly frightening situation during Bayern's 6-0 victory in a friendly with RB Leipzig on Saturday. Musiala began to look disorientated and started falling to the ground before two team-mates, Ismael Saibari and Joshua Kimmich, ran over to help.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



After the Heidenheim game, the Germany international revealed that he's been diagnosed with treatable absence seizures. "First things first - I'm doing fine," Musiala wrote on Instagram.

"I am particularly grateful for your messages and your support! I understand that many of you are worried. I want to put your minds at ease today and explain a few things: I have been diagnosed with temporary, brief, but well-treatable absences (absence seizures) caused by a neurological dysfunction.

"These can lead to the kind of moments that happened recently, such as against Leipzig or now in Heidenheim. I know these might look scary at first glance - but right now, they're just part of my daily life.

‌



View 3 Images Jamal Musiala was able to walk off the pitch (Image: EyesWideOpen/Getty Images)

"I am receiving the best possible medical care and am very optimistic. FC Bayern and my personal circle are always by my side, supporting me on this journey.

"Most importantly, there is no additional health risk beyond this. In close consultation and regular communication with experts, it was my personal wish to face this challenge and - with clearance from neurological specialists - to keep focusing on what helps my recovery most: simply living my everyday life and continuing to pursue my passion for playing football.

‌



"I have taken full responsibility for this decision. Overall, I feel very good about it and am on the right track. What helps me most on this path is to keep chasing victories and titles alongside my team and with your fantastic support.

View 3 Images Jamal Musiala collapsed for the second game in a row (Image: EyesWideOpen/Getty Images)

"I hope this helps you understand my situation better. At the same time, I kindly ask for your understanding that I wish to keep this matter private, within the circle of my closest confidants, the club, and the medical experts."
