Officials say it is funded by the Government of Liberia through the Public Sector Investment Program and is being executed under a design-and-build arrangement that the LNTA says will allow the final design to respond to site conditions, technical assessments and heritage-preservation requirements identified during the project’s initial phase.

But even as the government moves to transform the historic site into a major tourism destination, concerns have emerged over whether previous archaeological, heritage, environmental and technical studies have been adequately incorporated into the project and whether sufficient information has been made available to the public.

Providence Island, located in the heart of Monrovia, occupies a central place in Liberia’s history. It was the landing point for freed Black Americans in 1822 and became associated with the establishment of the settlement that eventually grew into Monrovia.

Twenty-five years later, Liberia declared independence, further cementing the island’s place in the country’s founding narrative.

Formerly known as Dozoa, the island lies between the Mesurado River and Stockton Creek, roughly 500 to 600 meters from the Atlantic Ocean’s bar mouth. Covering approximately 11.22 acres, the island has a distinctive guitar-like shape when viewed from above.

Over the years, the Liberian government has worked with international partners to document and preserve Providence Island’s historical significance. Those efforts have included archaeological investigations, heritage studies and preservation initiatives.

As the government embarks on a new redevelopment effort, however, questions are being raised about how those earlier findings will influence the project.

Calls for Greater Disclosure

FrontPage Africa contacted the LNTA following concerns raised by Liberian professionals and researchers, including architect and infrastructure systems consultant B. Garmondyu Zogar, who called for greater public disclosure of documents connected to the project.

Among the documents he said should be made available are the project feasibility study, master plan, Environmental and Social Impact Assessment, Heritage Impact Assessment, archaeological investigations, geotechnical and hydrological studies, environmental permits and procurement records.

The concerns are particularly significant because Providence Island has already been the subject of preservation and archaeological initiatives involving Liberian and international institutions.

U.S.-Liberia Preservation Initiative

FrontPage Africa established that Liberia and the United States signed a 2021 Memorandum of Understanding for a U.S.-Liberian Collaborative Initiative for the Preservation of Providence Island.

The initiative followed a nearly US$100,000 grant from the U.S. Department of State to the World Monuments Fund (WMF) through the Ambassador Fund for Cultural Preservation, under the oversight of the U.S. Embassy in Monrovia.

The grant supported research into the preservation and potential reuse of Providence Island. University of Virginia Professor Allison James was selected to lead the study and consulted Liberian stakeholders, including historian Dr. William B. Allen of the University of Liberia.

FrontPage Africa asked the LNTA whether it was aware of that research and whether its findings had been incorporated into the current redevelopment plans.

The Authority said it recognizes the body of work previously undertaken on the island.

“The Authority is aware that Providence Island has benefited from the involvement of a range of national and international institutions, historians, archaeologists, preservation specialists, development partners, and community stakeholders,” the LNTA said.

It added that the current project “is not intended to erase or disregard the history, archaeological record, or previous work undertaken on the Island.”

Raymond W. Stephens, Public Affairs Officer at the U.S. Embassy in Monrovia, said he was not at the Embassy when the agreement was signed and the study conducted.

However, he said Embassy staff who were present during the period told him the memorandum was between the World Monuments Fund and the Ministry of Information, Culture and Tourism.

According to Stephens, the Ambassador’s Fund for Cultural Preservation in Washington provided the funding, while the U.S. Embassy managed the funding process but was not directly involved in implementing the project.

He said the project was “entirely between WMF and MICAT” and that any final report would therefore have been submitted by the World Monuments Fund to the Ministry.

Thousands of Artifacts Recovered

The archaeological record of Providence Island has added another layer to the debate over its redevelopment.

Following the collapse of the island’s sacred cotton tree in 2019, members of the Back-to-Africa Heritage and Archaeology (BAHA) Project were invited to assist with salvage efforts.

That intervention developed into systematic archaeological research conducted over two seasons in 2022 and another season in 2023, in collaboration with the National Museum of Liberia.

The work resulted in the recovery of thousands of artifacts now in the custody of the National Museum.

Some of the artifacts reportedly predate the arrival of the settlers in 1822, suggesting that human activity on Providence Island extends beyond the conventional narrative surrounding Liberia’s founding.

The archaeological surveys also identified the island’s original extent, areas with high concentrations of artifacts and sections considered particularly vulnerable to coastal erosion.

BAHA has said its work was conducted in consultation with the team associated with the World Monuments Fund, including landscape architects at Studio Zewde.

Researchers, community elders and other stakeholders subsequently developed what BAHA described as a long-term plan for the island.

The plan sought to protect the island’s archaeological heritage while maintaining public access and recognizing both the 1822 settlement and Indigenous use of Providence Island before and after the settlement.

FrontPage Africa asked the LNTA whether it is engaging with BAHA, whether it is aware of the archaeological findings, and whether BAHA, the National Museum, World Monuments Fund, Studio Zewde, or other heritage experts were consulted in preparing the current redevelopment plan.

The LNTA did not provide specific responses to each question but said the redevelopment would build on existing research and involve relevant institutions and stakeholders.

“The relevant studies will build upon existing research, historical records, technical studies, and other available information, supplemented by additional investigations where required,” the Authority said.

It also acknowledged the importance of the archaeological discoveries.

“The LNTA acknowledges the significance of archaeological findings reportedly recovered from Providence Island and the importance of ensuring that archaeological resources are appropriately protected throughout project implementation,” it said.

LNTA: Physical Construction Will Follow Studies, Approvals

The LNTA said the Providence Island Development Project is being implemented as a Design & Build project procured under IF No. LNTA/SP/NCB/001/2026.

According to the Authority, Phase I of the contract will focus on the technical studies, investigations and detailed designs necessary to establish the engineering and regulatory foundation for the project.

The studies are expected to include topographical and site surveys, geotechnical investigations, hydrological and drainage assessments, structural and civil engineering studies, environmental and social assessments, heritage and archaeological investigations, as well as other pre-construction assessments.

The LNTA stressed that the anticipated September 2026 commencement does not mean physical construction will begin before the required studies and approvals are completed.

“Consequently, the anticipated September 2026 commencement should be understood within the phased sequencing of the Design-Build contract and should not be interpreted to mean that physical construction will proceed without the requisite detailed studies, designs, statutory approvals, licenses, and permits,” the Authority said.

It said approvals and permits will be obtained from the Ministry of Public Works, Environmental Protection Agency and other competent government institutions before physical construction begins.

The Design-Build team, the LNTA added, will work with government institutions, technical agencies, environmental authorities, heritage institutions and other stakeholders to identify and incorporate environmental, social, heritage and archaeological safeguards into the final designs and construction methodology.

Public Review Promised

The LNTA said it intends to organize public engagements after Phase I is completed and the necessary approvals obtained.

Those engagements, according to the Authority, will present the findings of the technical studies and detailed engineering designs and provide an opportunity for public and professional review before construction begins.

The Authority said the ultimate goal is to transform Providence Island into a major national heritage and tourism destination without compromising its historical and cultural value.

LNTA Defends Procurement

Beyond heritage concerns, questions have also been raised about how the project was procured.

The LNTA said the project went through a competitive public procurement process in accordance with Liberia’s procurement laws and under the oversight framework of the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission.

The Invitation for Bids, the Authority said, was advertised in four local daily newspapers and online.

Seven companies purchased the bidding documents, which the LNTA cited as evidence of competitive market interest.

The Authority said the Design-Build contract was processed in accordance with required procurement procedures and received the requisite “no-objections.”

However, in its response to FrontPage Africa, the LNTA did not provide copies of the feasibility study, master plan, environmental assessment, heritage assessment or other procurement records requested by the newspaper.

Instead, it maintained that several of the technical studies in question will form part of Phase I of the Design-Build contract.

Balancing Development and Preservation

The planned redevelopment places the government at the intersection of two competing demands: transforming Providence Island into a more accessible and economically productive tourism destination while preserving the historical and archaeological evidence embedded beneath and around the site.

For heritage advocates and researchers, the concern is that development could permanently alter a site whose significance extends beyond the arrival of settlers in 1822.

For the LNTA, however, the redevelopment represents an opportunity to provide Providence Island with the infrastructure and management needed to establish it as a major national heritage and tourism destination.

The Authority maintains that development and preservation can proceed together.

“Constructive dialogue is important, particularly where the protection of Liberia’s national heritage is concerned,” the LNTA said, extending an invitation to researchers, historians, archaeologists, heritage professionals, institutions and other interested parties to engage with the Authority.

Still, with the project expected to move into its next phase in September, questions remain over which previous studies will ultimately influence the final design, how archaeological discoveries will be protected and whether the public and heritage experts will have meaningful input before irreversible changes are made to one of Liberia’s most important historical sites.

For a country whose modern political history is inseparable from Providence Island, the success of the redevelopment may ultimately be measured not only by what is built there, but by what is preserved.

World.title: Liberia: As National Elections Commission Chief Steps Down After 12 Years, Advocates Say She Offers a Powerful Example of Women’s Leadership
World.content:
Davidetta Browne Lansanah providing an update in the runup to the 2023 elections.

Summary:

Advocates said Davidetta Browne Lansanah, who stepped down after 12 successful years leading the National Elections Commission in March, showed the positive impact of women’s leadership in Liberia.

Lansanah joins other examples of women leading with results, from former president Ellen Johnson Sirleaf to women peacebuilders and those now serving in government.

The question now, said advocates, is whether Liberians will turn those examples into a political opportunity for more women. Advocates said a bill before the Legislature that would require parties to put women up for 30 percent of seats is the test.

When Davidetta Browne Lansanah stood down from her role at the helm of the National Elections Commission in March, after 12 years on the job, she carried with her a record that women’s rights advocates said should settle once and for all an old argument in Liberia: women can lead.

By Joyclyn Wea, gender correspondent with New Narratives

At the Commission, Lansanah worked through 2 presidential elections, disputed results, political pressure, and one of the closest presidential races in Liberia’s recent history when President Joseph Boakai defeated former President George Weah by fewer than 21,000 votes. Advocates said the fact that the country accepted the result and moved on peacefully was a testament to the people’s trust in Lansanah’s leadership.

In an interview with FrontPage Africa/New Narratives, Lansanah said that she should never have been in doubt.

“Females have quality,” Lansanah said. “Females can run any institution. I am a living demonstration of that.”

Lansanah submitted her resignation to President Boakai, choosing to leave one year early to rest because she had worked for 12 years without leave. She was replaced by Jonathan K. Weedor, who served over 16 years as a commissioner and acting co-chairman.

Lansanah was appointed to the Commission during the administration of former President Sirleaf and stayed on under former President Weah and President Boakai. She helped guide the Commission through difficult elections and public pressure. She said she did the work with discipline and commitment.

Advocates said Lansanah’s 12 years at the Commission left a strong legacy. They point to the 2023 election as a serious test not just for the Commission but of Lansanah’s leadership. Political tensions were high. But the process ended without the kind of crisis many Liberians feared.

“She has a record that will live on,” said Malcolm Joseph, chairman of the Elections Coordinating Committee, Liberia’s largest domestic election observer group. “In other countries, that kind of close election could have been resisted and led to something else.”

Lansanah said she is proud of the role she played. But she said her biggest achievement was not only the elections she helped manage. It was also the people she helped build inside the Commission.

She said the technical staff at the Commission is capable, hardworking, and ready to do more with the support they need.

“If you ignore them, you will fail,” she said.

On women’s leadership, Lansanah said the issue is simple: Liberia cannot continue to say women are capable while leaving the political system almost entirely in the hands of men. Her own career, she said, should help answer the question of whether women can handle serious public responsibility.

In April the Legislative session passed the amendment to provisions within the new election law, including the 30 percent gender quota for political parties.

Her departure comes at a time when Liberia is again debating how much space should be reserved for women in politics. The most recent elections delivered a Legislature where less than 11 percent were women. Electors had few women to vote for because they were nominated for few of the seats.

Liberian electorates in long queues to vote in the October 10 polls. Credit. World Press

The House of Representatives has passed an electoral reform bill with one provision that would require political parties to include at least 30 percent women on their candidate lists for legislative elections. It’s modeled on laws in other countries in Africa that have seen significantly higher representation by women. Most countries with fast-growing economies have high representation of women in the legislatures.

But the bill is not yet law. It has been in the Senate since May. It was not passed before the Legislative break as legislators continue to debate elements of the bill.

For many women’s rights advocates, the debate is not only about fairness. It is also about results.

Davidetta Browne-Lansanah turned over transition note to her successor Jonathan Weedor, in March.

Liberia has already seen women lead at the highest level. Former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf became the first woman elected president in Africa. Women also played a major role in pushing for peace during Liberia’s civil war. To date, President Boakai has appointed 8 women to his 20-member cabinet. At a women’s town hall meeting in July 2024, he praised women’s leadership, saying the women he had appointed were “capable and they are performing.” He added, “This is why we need more and more women.”

Experts said Sirleaf’s presidency also gave an example of what women’s leadership could deliver after war. Though critics cite her reluctance to prosecute corrupt officials and failure to implement Truth and Reconciliation Commission recommendations, her administration secured major debt relief, rebuilt relations with international partners, restored some basic services, and kept the country on a path of peace after years of conflict. In 2011, the international community celebrated her achievements when she shared the Nobel Peace Prize with Liberian peace activist Leymah Gbowee and Yemen’s Tawakkol Karman for their work for women’s rights and women’s role in peacebuilding.

But advocates said appointments are not enough.

Cabinet ministers serve at the will of the president. Lawmakers, on the other hand, are elected by the people. They write laws, approve budgets, and represent communities. That is where women remain badly underrepresented.

In the 73-member House of Representatives, only eight lawmakers are women. In the Senate, women hold only three of the 30 seats. That means men still control most of the decisions by the Legislature.

The numbers from the last election show how hard it is for women to even get on the ballot.

Last year, political parties signed a revised MoU with the NEC To Strengthen Electoral Cooperation. Credit: United Nations Development Program

In 2023, only 152 of 1,030 candidates for the House of Representatives were women, according to the Electoral Institute for Sustainable Democracy in Africa. Only seven women ran for the Senate out of 100 candidates. Only two political parties met the 30 percent target for women candidates.

That is why Lansanah said she spent years calling for a stronger law.

Liberia’s election law already tells political parties to “endeavor to ensure” that at least 30 percent of their candidates are women. But there is no punishment for parties that fail to do so. Women’s groups said that language has allowed parties to promise support for women while still leaving them off their tickets.

The new bill passed by the House is meant to change that. It said political parties should submit candidate lists with at least 30 percent women. Supporters said it could help increase the number of women in the Legislature and give voters more choices.

But the bill has also caused concern.

Women’s groups said the current version still leaves an escape route for political parties. Under the bill, the Electoral Commission may accept a party’s list if the party shows “good cause” that, despite its “best efforts,” it could not meet the 30 percent requirement.

To many advocates, that sounds too much like the old law. They want the Senate to remove the “good cause” and “best efforts” language and require parties that fall short to correct their lists or face consequences.

“That’s not enforceable,” said Representative Ellen Attoh-Wreh, chair of the Women’s Legislative Caucus of Liberia. “If parties can simply convince the Commission they tried, then the quota becomes optional.”

Lansanah said she plans to rest, finish law school, and find another way to serve Liberia. But she said she is not leaving the fight for women’s leadership.

Her message to the country is the same one she carried out of the Commission: Liberia has already seen what women can do when they are trusted with power.

Now, she said, it is time to make room for more of them.

World.title: Kafwaya’s whereabouts still unknown as HRC widens inquiry
World.content:
The Human Rights Commission is calling on the Zambia Police Service and other law enforcement agencies to urgently clarify the whereabouts of former Lunte Member of Parliament Mutotwe Kafwaya, whose family says he has been missing since 14 August.

The Commission says that if Kafwaya is in lawful state custody, his place of detention should be disclosed to ensure due process is followed without hindrance. It says he is entitled to unhindered access to his family and legal representatives under established minimum human rights standards.

The Commission has been following up on reports concerning Kafwaya’s whereabouts since Sunday, 16 August. Investigators have visited Chelstone, Matero, Lusaka Central and Kabwata police stations, where they were informed he is not in their custody.

The Zambia Police command has not provided any further information on the matter, the Commission said. As of Tuesday, 18 August, it committed to extending its inquiries to Chilenje, Twin Palm and Woodlands police stations, and to continue engaging investigators at Zambia Police Service headquarters. It has pledged to provide an update as further inquiries progress.

The Commission’s intervention follows days of conflicting accounts over Kafwaya’s condition and location, none of which have been independently verified.

The matter traces back to an armed security operation at the Kabulonga residence of presidential candidate Brian Mundubile around 14 and 15 August. NRPUP running mate Makebi Zulu alleged on social media that Kafwaya had been shot twice in the chest by military personnel and was in critical condition at Maina Soko Military Hospital. Zulu also named three other individuals he said were detained at Central Police, and said the whereabouts of others involved in the operation remained unknown.

Government swiftly and categorically denied the claim. Defence Permanent Secretary Maambo Haamaundu said the Ministry of Defence had verified with Maina Soko Military Hospital management and found no record of any patient named Kafwaya admitted there in the preceding 48 hours.

Information and Media Permanent Secretary Thabo Kawana echoed the denial, describing the circulating reports as false and warning that government was monitoring the spread of misinformation during what he called a sensitive post-election period. Kawana directly challenged Kafwaya to come forward and clarify his own whereabouts.

Kafwaya’s wife, Dinis Ngandu Kafwaya, has given her own account of the days since he disappeared. In a video statement, she said she last spoke to her husband by phone around midday on Friday, 14 August, and that by 17:00 that evening her calls to him had gone unanswered, with his phone continuing to ring without being picked up.

She has also said she was denied access when she went to Maina Soko Military Hospital to check on his condition, a claim that sits alongside, but has not resolved, the ministry’s denial that he was ever admitted there.

The family broke its public silence more fully on 16 August, when Kafwaya’s son, Mwanga Kafwaya, and his elder brother, Mugupa Musuma, speaking as family spokesperson, appealed directly to President Hakainde Hichilema for help establishing Kafwaya’s whereabouts and safety.

Mwanga said he had last spoken to his father on Wednesday, 12 August, and had had no contact with him since. He said the family’s concern was focused squarely on his father’s life, safety and location, rather than on assigning blame or engaging with speculation.

Musuma called on the President, the Zambia Police Service and the Zambia Army to assist in locating Kafwaya.

Mundubile’s party, NRPUP, has separately called for an independent inquiry into the Kabulonga operation. It has demanded immediate access by lawyers, relatives, medical personnel and independent human rights monitors to anyone arrested, detained or injured during the operation, along with preservation of CCTV footage, operational logs, radio communications, weapons records, vehicle movement records and detention logs.

The party has also asked whether any extraordinary security directive or state of emergency was in force to authorise the deployment of armed personnel against political figures, a question government has not directly addressed.

Government has confirmed that 11 Tonse Alliance-aligned individuals were arrested in connection with the period surrounding the operation, saying they were found in possession of high-grade military weapons allegedly intended to threaten state security. Those named by government include Tonse Alliance presidential spokesperson George Chisanga, Patrick Mwansa, Bishop Trevor Mwamba, Simon Phiri, Richard Banda and Francis Mulenga.

Chisanga’s continued detention without charge at Chelston Police Station since 14 August has been separately confirmed by his family, who are pursuing habeas corpus proceedings through the High Court.

Home Affairs and Internal Security Minister Dickson Matembo has warned that individuals making what he called alarming claims during this period would be required to account for their statements.

As things stand, Kafwaya’s location, physical condition and legal status remain unconfirmed by any independent source. The claim that he was shot originates solely with Zulu’s social media statement and has not been corroborated; government’s denial that he was hospitalised at Maina Soko has likewise not been independently verified beyond the ministry’s own account.

The Human Rights Commission’s ongoing station-by-station search represents the first institutionally independent effort to establish where Kafwaya is, separate from the competing claims of government and opposition figures. Its next update is expected once inquiries at Chilenje, Twin Palm, Woodlands and police headquarters are complete.

World.title: Kalaba praises Mundubile’s fight, demands independent election review
World.content:
Citizens First president Harry Kalaba has commended Tonse Alliance leader Brian Mundubile for what he called a “spirited and courageous fight” in the August general election, while demanding an independent review of a process he described as deeply flawed.

In a statement issued on 19 August, Kalaba praised Mundubile for standing firm under what he alleged were conditions of intimidation, provocation and systemic irregularities. He said this required resilience and an unwavering commitment to democratic principles.

Kalaba also commended ordinary Zambians for their conduct after the 13 August polls. He said citizens chose restraint over chaos and dignity over disorder, despite what he described as clear provocation and a worrying departure from established election management standards.

The Citizens First leader did not stop at praise. He said the process raised serious concerns that could not be ignored.

He cited reports of intimidation, interference with polling processes, and inconsistencies in the handling of electoral materials. He also pointed to what he called the uneven application of the law during the election period.

Kalaba said these issues fell short of the democratic standards Zambia has historically upheld. He warned that the country’s international standing was now at risk.

“Zambia was once regarded as a beacon of stability, democracy and good governance on the African continent,” Kalaba said. He warned that the country now risks being seen as a cautionary tale rather than a model for the region.

He said Zambia was in danger of becoming, in his words, a laughing stock both regionally and globally. Kalaba insisted this was not a label the Zambian people deserved.

The Citizens First leader placed responsibility for restoring credibility squarely on the institutions that manage elections. He said those institutions must rise above reproach.

“The integrity of whom the people choose must be protected not only in outcome, but in process,” Kalaba said. He argued that without this, the legitimacy of governance itself would remain in question.

Kalaba reaffirmed his party’s commitment to peaceful democratic engagement going forward. He said Citizens First would continue advocating for transparency, accountability and protection of the sovereign will of Zambians.

He called for a thorough, transparent and independent review of the electoral process. Kalaba said this was necessary so that the concerns raised could be addressed and public confidence restored.

He offered a broader reflection on what democracy should mean in practice. “Democracy is not merely about putting an ‘X’ on paper,” Kalaba said. “It is about ensuring that every individual is free to choose whomever they wish, and that their choice is protected from interference.”

Kalaba closed his statement on a unifying note, saying Zambia belongs to all its citizens. He said the country must work together to reclaim and restore the democratic values that define it as a nation.

The Citizens First leader also addressed the human cost of the election period directly. He extended condolences to the families of those who lost loved ones before, during and after the polls, without specifying names or numbers.

Kalaba additionally demanded that government issue a comprehensive statement regarding former Lunte member of Parliament Mutotwe Kafwaya. This follows continued uncertainty over Kafwaya’s circumstances, with his wife having previously sought information about his whereabouts.

The Zambia Police Service has said it is waiting for government to issue a statement on Kafwaya’s status, with spokesperson Godfrey Chilabi confirming the police would stick to guidance provided by Secretary to Cabinet Patrick Kangwa. Kalaba said transparency on the Kafwaya matter would be a good starting point for the national healing he believes the country now needs.

Kalaba’s intervention adds to a growing chorus of opposition-aligned voices questioning aspects of the election’s conduct. Transparency International Zambia has separately flagged process concerns in 16 of 117 assessed constituencies, citing unsealed ballot papers and delays in issuing result forms, though the organisation’s own parallel monitoring found no material difference from the results announced by the Electoral Commission of Zambia.

Political analyst Dr Neo Simutanyi has also argued that the opposition has strong legal grounds to petition the outcome, citing disputed results and alleged electoral violence in several constituencies. Mundubile himself has said his party will pursue legal redress over what NRPUP alleges were irregularities in the handling of ballot security and electoral materials.

Government has not yet responded directly to Kalaba’s statement. President Hakainde Hichilema, in his acceptance speech following the declaration of results, urged citizens to reject the use of militias or violence in pursuit of public office and pledged to serve all Zambians regardless of how they voted.

Kalaba’s statement did not name individuals or provide documentary evidence for the specific allegations of intimidation and interference he referenced. The claims remain, at this stage, allegations advanced by an opposition party leader rather than findings established by any investigative or judicial body.

World.title: Hichilema Pledges To Serve All Zambians, Warns Against Armed Militias In Victory Address
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema used his first address to the nation since being declared winner of the presidential election to pledge to serve all Zambians equally, thank the more than 80,000 people who worked to deliver the vote, and issue a pointed warning against what he called “bands of armed militias” operating in the country.

Speaking with what he described as profound humility and gratitude, Hichilema said the mandate given to him represented a decision by millions of Zambians who had once again chosen to settle their political differences peacefully. “We had citizens, I think numbering over 80,000 in total, or thereabouts, working to deliver this election,” he said, thanking both the officials involved and the wider public for what he called a demonstration of democratic maturity.

The president was emphatic that his government would not distinguish between those who voted for him and those who did not. “Those who voted for us, those who didn’t, you’re equal citizens,” he said. “There’s no discriminatory understanding of who voted and their favour. Those who didn’t vote for us, they are not favoured.” He extended that message directly to supporters of rival candidates, saying anyone who backed a different contender “is not your enemy,” but rather “your brother, they are your sister, your uncle, auntie, they are your neighbour.”

Hichilema devoted a substantial part of his address to what he described as concrete gains delivered over his first term. He said the number of pupils per teacher had fallen steadily as government recruitment continued, and that close to 2.6 million children, including teenage mothers who had previously dropped out, had returned to school under free education. “Education is the best investment,” he said. “It’s the best equaliser.”

On the economy, the president pointed to debt restructuring as a signature achievement, saying it had freed up close to $1.9 billion a year previously lost to debt servicing. He said that money was now being redirected toward government programmes. He also cited what he called Zambia’s first-ever harvest of 5 million metric tons of maize, and said the Food Reserve Agency was now paying farmers for their crop within two to three days of delivery, a turnaround he said had never happened before.

The president struck a firmer tone when he turned to questions of law and order, delivering some of his most direct remarks of the address. “We should not allow our country to degenerate into bands of armed militias,” he said. “At that point, that’s crossing the line. Because once you start doing those things, you are injuring others. You are endangering the lives of others.” He said any pursuit of public office through what he termed “malicious” means, rather than genuine service, was “alien to us” and should be rejected outright by citizens.

He also appealed directly to supporters on both sides of the contest to avoid celebrations that could spill into confrontation. “Let us be responsible at all times,” he said, urging Zambians not to provoke those celebrating the result and warning against any action that could injure people or damage property. “There is no winner here. There’s no loser. We are all winners. Zambia is the winner,” he said.

Hichilema also addressed public sector workers directly, telling health workers in particular that patients deserved full attention rather than distraction. “Let’s agree that you will not go to a ward and start playing with your phone when the patient is screaming in pain,” he said, describing the exchange as one he recalled from a campaign stop. He called for a broader shift in national work culture, arguing that productivity, not just agriculture, would drive the country’s development, and urged citizens toward what he called hard work over what he described as laziness.

The president closed his address with an appeal for national unity and a prayer for the country, invoking Zambia’s founding motto. “There’s only one Zambia. One country. One destiny,” he said. “One Zambia, one nation, one people. That’s what we are.” He said his government would continue to treat every Zambian’s wellbeing as its responsibility regardless of how they voted, and pledged that his household would remain accountable to what he called the country’s 21 million citizens.

The address, delivered as the country continues to work through a disputed election period, made no direct reference to the ongoing legal and security disputes raised by opposition candidate Brian Mundubile, focusing instead on reconciliation, service delivery and calls for calm.

World.title: Hichilema Won’t Be Sworn In Yet, We Are Petitioning, Says Mundubile
World.content:
NRPUP presidential candidate Brian Mundubile says President Hakainde Hichilema will not be sworn in yet, as he prepares a legal challenge against the declared election results.

Mundubile insists he did not lose the election and says he is ready to take the matter to court, where he believes the evidence will expose what he describes as a rigged process. He maintains his Parallel Voter Tabulation and results collected by his G20 teams point to serious irregularities, particularly in Southern, North-Western and Western provinces.

Speaking on the challenge he intends to mount, Mundubile was direct about where he believes the numbers do not hold up. “We are challenging the announcement of results because we believe we have sufficient grounds to prove that this election was rigged,” he said. “Southern, Western and North-Western provinces are areas of concern. We have the G20’s that prove that we won the elections.”

His campaign’s grievances extend beyond those three provinces. A claim circulating on social media this week alleges that ECZ’s certified win for Hichilema in the Wusakile constituency understates the true result, asserting Mundubile actually polled 17,274 votes against 7,800 for Hichilema there. ECZ’s certified figures for Wusakile, which match independently compiled constituency data, give Hichilema 22,273 votes against 17,196 for Mundubile. The alternative figures have not been supported by any polling-station form, agent’s tally sheet or other documentation, and their source has not been identified, so they remain an unverified allegation rather than an established fact.

The dispute has taken on a more serious dimension in recent days. Mundubile says he was forced into hiding after unknown men broke into his property and opened fire at people there, an incident that has already drawn conflicting accounts from his camp and the government. He says the threats did not stop afterwards, leaving him with no choice but to seek protection at the United Nations compound.

Mundubile has now addressed that incident directly for the first time, firmly rejecting government claims that a militia had been present at his home. “I want to put it very clear on record, there was no presence of any militia at my home,” he said in an interview. Asked whether he had been arrested and charged, he said he was detained briefly but never formally charged. “I had been picked and later released. I was not charged at all,” he said.

He gave a detailed account of what he says happened when armed personnel arrived at the property. “Upon arrival at our residence, they began to shoot. They shot through the guardhouse. They knocked the gate down using an armoured vehicle. They broke down the doors, broke the windows and gate access,” he said. Mundubile said he was in the same room as former Lunte MP Mutotwe Kafwaya when the shooting began. “Three soldiers broke in and immediately opened fire at Honourable Kafwaya. He later directed that gun towards me and fired two shots. Later, he fired at the wardrobe where my wife was,” he said, adding that physical evidence remained at the property. “We can literally go to visit the site and see exactly what I’m talking about.”

Pressed on his earlier claim that colleagues had died in the raid, Mundubile acknowledged he could not confirm this independently. “It’s still unknown,” he said. “I insisted to them, I pleaded with them to take me to the hospital because he had been bleeding and we were being dragged like animals out of that house.” On the government’s assertion that high-grade weapons were recovered at the residence, he was equally direct. “We were not armed at all. Honourable Kafwaya was not armed. My wife was not armed. I was not armed,” he said, suggesting any firearms found on his security personnel would have been ordinary civilian-licensed weapons. “There’ll be no dangerous weapon that they can display to the world to confirm that they found dangerous weapons,” he said.

The declaration opens a new and potentially volatile chapter in the election dispute, with the country now waiting to see whether the courts will be asked to formally examine the evidence Mundubile says his teams have gathered. A legal challenge of this kind, if filed, would place Zambia’s judiciary at the centre of resolving a contest that has already spilled well beyond the counting halls.

Not everyone is convinced the numbers support Mundubile’s case. An electoral expert has poured cold water on the claim, arguing that even if Hichilema’s entire Southern Province vote were removed from his total, Mundubile would still fall short of the votes needed to win outright. That assessment cuts against the heart of Mundubile’s argument, which rests on the idea that irregularities in a handful of provinces were enough to flip the national result. Whether his legal team can produce evidence strong enough to overcome that arithmetic gap is likely to become the central question if the matter reaches court.

Mundubile’s account of the raid continues to conflict directly with statements from the Ministry of Defence, which has previously described allegations that Kafwaya was shot and later died as “a total fabrication,” and with Cabinet Secretary Patrick Kangwa‘s earlier assertion that the operation was linked to an alleged militia at the property. Neither side’s account has been independently verified.

For now, the standoff leaves Zambia in an unusual position. The Electoral Commission has certified Hichilema as winner with a result well above the threshold required to avoid a run-off, yet the man he defeated is refusing to accept that outcome and is actively preparing to contest it through the courts, all while reportedly sheltering from threats to his safety and disputing the government’s account of the raid on his home.

The battle may therefore be far from over. The next showdown could now move from the polling stations to the courtroom, with both sides likely to face pressure to produce hard evidence rather than competing claims. Zambian electoral law gives candidates a window to formally petition a presidential result, and Mundubile’s public remarks suggest he intends to use it.

What happens next will depend heavily on what documentation each side is willing to put before a court, and how quickly. Party agents, legal teams and election watchers across the country are now bracing for that process to begin in earnest.

World.title: The Numbers Do Not Add Up: Zambia Has A Serious Election Problem
World.content:
By Brian Matambo, Media Director, PF Pamodzi Alliance

There is now a serious problem with the results of Zambia’s 13 August election, and it does not require complicated mathematics to understand. Let me use myself as an example.

On election day, I went to vote at Kabulonga Boys. I joined the queue, waited my turn, and presented my NRC and voter’s card to the polling assistant. She called out my name, my NRC number and my voter’s card number, checked them against the voters’ register, and confirmed them.

I received four ballot papers: one for President, one for Member of Parliament, one for Mayor, and one for Councillor. I went into the booth, marked an X against my preferred candidate in each of the four elections, and deposited each ballot into its corresponding box before leaving the polling station.

That is how millions of Zambians voted. So here is the question: how can there be dramatically more presidential votes than parliamentary votes from people who went through the same process at the same time?

Small differences are normal. Someone may decide not to vote for an MP. A ballot may be spoiled. There will always be exceptions. But this is not a story about a few ballots.

An analysis published by The Africa Report found large differences between presidential and parliamentary turnout in a number of constituencies. In just 16 constituencies examined, the gap reportedly exceeded 170,000 votes.

In Solwezi North, the difference between presidential and parliamentary turnout is reported at more than 46 percentage points. That question needs an answer.

The analysis also identified at least 27 constituencies where presidential turnout exceeded 80 percent, against a national registered-voter-weighted turnout of approximately 57 percent. Nine of those constituencies are in North-Western Province, eight in Western Province, six in Southern Province, three in rural Copperbelt, and one in Central Province. The analysis found none in Eastern, Luapula, Muchinga or Northern provinces, the areas where the opposition performed strongly.

This is where the problem becomes more serious. If people entered a polling station, were verified against the same voters’ register, and participated in elections held at the same time, the ballot papers should reconcile.

If the presidential ballot box contains substantially more votes than the parliamentary race, somebody has to explain where that difference came from. We cannot simply announce results and move on. Where did those presidential votes come from? What happened to the corresponding parliamentary ballots?

These are not opposition questions. They are mathematical questions, and mathematics does not belong to UPND, NRPUP, Tonse Pamodzi or anybody else. The numbers either reconcile or they do not.

The Africa Report estimates that the suspicious difference between presidential and parliamentary turnout could represent somewhere between 350,000 and 550,000 votes nationally, though the publication itself describes this estimate as unverified.

Even that figure would not, on its own, wipe out the approximately 1.1 million-vote difference in the presidential result announced by ECZ. But if this happened in a UPND stronghold, it is reasonable to ask whether votes for Brian Mundubile were reduced or tampered with elsewhere in NRPUP strongholds.

This is only one method of testing the integrity of the election. It does not tell us whether there were other irregularities. It does not resolve allegations about monitors being removed from polling stations. It does not answer questions about results forms. It does not explain what happened during the suspension of counting. And it does not resolve the wider concerns surrounding the electoral environment, including allegations of the army being used to intimidate the public.

So before anybody tells Zambians to accept these results and move on, let us first reconcile the numbers. Bring out the polling-station results. Bring out the GEN 20 forms. Bring out the ballot-paper accounts. Bring out the voters’ registers. Then let us compare the presidential vote against the parliamentary vote, polling station by polling station, constituency by constituency.

This should not frighten anybody who believes the election was clean. I know what happened when I voted at Kabulonga Boys, because I was there. I was verified once, I received my ballots, I voted, and I deposited them into their respective boxes before leaving.

Multiply my experience by millions of Zambians, and the discrepancies become difficult to ignore. If the numbers reconcile, let the evidence show it.

But if they do not, and if hundreds of thousands of presidential votes cannot be satisfactorily accounted for against the other elections conducted at the same time, then Zambia has a bigger problem than a disputed result. We have a compromised election.

If these discrepancies are confirmed, the demand for a fresh presidential election will not simply be a political demand. It will be the logical consequence of numbers that do not add up.

World.title: Ruto, Hassan and Ndayishimiye congratulate HH
World.content:
Kenyan President William Ruto, Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu Hassan and Burundi President Evariste Ndayishimiye have congratulated President Hakainde Hichilema on his re-election.

President Ruto, in a congratulatory message dated August 18, 2026, extended his congratulations on behalf of the Kenyan Government and the people, describing Mr Hichilema’s victory as a testament to his dedication, perseverance and commitment to Zambia’s advancement.

Mr Ruto said the election result was an affirmation of the trust and confidence the Zambian people had placed in President Hichilema’s leadership to advance national development and prosperity.

He said Kenya attaches great importance to its relations with Zambia, noting that the two countries have maintained deep and enduring cooperation at bilateral and multilateral levels.

ZANIS reports that President Ruto also described Zambia as a brotherly nation, valuable partner and ally in the region, further expressing his desire to work closely with President Hichilema to strengthen and broaden the bonds of friendship and cooperation between the two countries.

He has wished President Hichilema success during his second term as well as peace, unity and prosperity for the people of Zambia.

And, President Hassan has also congratulated President Hichilema, describing Tanzania’s relations with Zambia as deep, historical and fraternal.

In a message posted on her official social media account on X, President Hassan extended heartfelt congratulations to President Hichilema on his re-election.

She said she looked forward to continuing to work with President Hichilema to strengthen the bilateral ties between Tanzania and Zambia for the benefit of the two nations.

President Hassan also conveyed her best wishes to President Hichilema and Zambia, while invoking blessings for Zambia and Africa.

Meanwhile, President Ndayishimiye who is also Chairperson of the African Union (AU), conveyed his message of congratulations via a social media post on X.

He wished continued success for President Hichilema as he leads the Zambian people towards greater peace, unity and prosperity, for the benefit of Zambia and the African continent as a whole.

World.title: President Hichilema addresses Zambians after being re-elected
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has called on the Zambian people to respect divergent views and safeguard the country’s democracy, saying differences in opinion should never degenerate into violence.

President Hichilema says democracy thrives when citizens allow one another to express different views peacefully.

He noted that there is no justification for people to turn and resort to ‘militias’, cause violence, turn to street fights, destroy public property or other forms of lawlessness whenever they disagree with others.

The President-elect was speaking in his re-election acceptance speech, broadcast live on ZNBC radio and television.

Today, Electoral Commission of Zambia Chairperson Mwangala Zaloumis declared Mr Hichilema duly elected Head of State after he defeated 11 others in the August 13, general elections.

President Hichilema thanked the Zambian people who voted for him or not, including those in the ruling UPND candidates, opposition and independent candidates in the just ended general elections.

He urged citizens to protect public and private assets, saying such resources are critical to sustaining livelihoods and providing opportunities for future generations.

He said Zambia belongs to all citizens and there are no winners or losers in an election, but only one Zambia, one nation and one people with a common destiny.

The Head of State also called for peace, justice, law and order, stressing that lawlessness has no room in the country.

Mr Hichilema said Zambians should reject the use of violence and malicious activities as a means of seeking public office, describing such practices as alien to the country’s values.

He further urged elected leaders at all levels to serve the people with humility and put national interests ahead of personal interests.

He said those elected like him, members of parliament, mayors, council chairpersons and councillors should always remember that public office is a responsibility to serve citizens.

And Mr Hichilema also called on Zambians to embrace hard work and productivity, saying the country should not only be a nation of traders but also of producers.

He stressed that productivity should be promoted across all sectors, including agriculture, manufacturing, education, health and the public service.

Mr Hichilema urged public service workers to take their responsibilities seriously and deliver services efficiently, warning against neglecting duties while using public resources.

He cited health workers as an example, saying medical personnel should treat patients with care and professionalism because they too may one day require medical services.

The President-elect assured that government will continue creating opportunities for citizens through investment, economic growth and skills development.

Mr Hichilema said the next five years will focus on economic growth through increased investment, job creation, business opportunities and increased government revenue.

He said economic growth will help government address the cost of living and improve the welfare of vulnerable citizens.

He cited free education, Constituency Development Fund (CDF) and skills training programmes as some of the measures the government has implemented to reduce the cost of living and expand opportunities.

Mr Hichilema said CDF has also enabled communities to access bursaries and skills training, while creating opportunities for local people to participate in development projects.

He said the country’s development agenda should benefit every community and household, adding that development is a process and not an event.

He further said the new proportional representation system will create opportunities for more women, youths and persons with disabilities to participate in Parliament.

The President-elect thanked God for preserving the lives of Zambians and called on citizens to continue supporting one another, particularly during difficult times.

Mr Hichilema said Zambia should remain united and peaceful as it works towards achieving a better life for all.

World.title: Solwezi Clergy calls for unity after general elections
World.content:
A clergyman in Solwezi District has called for unity of purpose following the just ended August 2026, general elections.

Catholic Diocese of Solwezi Priest Christopher Sawila says now that the elections have been concluded and leaders elected, citizens should shift their focus towards rebuilding communities and promoting sustainable development.

Father Sawila told the media in an interview today that the period of political campaigns, rallies and intense debates has come to an end, making it necessary for citizens to concentrate on development.

He said that although elections provide an opportunity for citizens to consider different perspectives and competing visions for the country’s future, the conclusion of the electoral process should mark the beginning of collective efforts towards national development.

“The season of campaigns, political rallies, and intense debate has come to an end. As the dust settles across the country, the moment has arrived to shift our collective focus from the campaign trail to the essential work of community building and sustainable development,” he said.

Fr Sawila said both elected leaders and those who were not elected have a role to play in promoting unity and serving the interests of citizens.

He said North-Western Province has vast opportunities as well as challenges that require collective efforts beyond political party lines.

“North-Western Province holds vast economic potential, from its expanding mining and agricultural sectors to rich natural resources and vibrant trade communities.

Maximizing these resources to improve infrastructure, health services, and education requires input and commitment from across the political spectrum,” he added.

Fr Sawila said development is a shared responsibility that requires constructive dialogue, accountability and criticism where necessary.

He has since called on newly elected leaders to govern inclusively, while urging those in opposition to provide constructive criticism and contribute to the development of the province and the nation.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 19, 2026
World.content:
Zimbabwe Identifies 39 More Kariba Boat Tragedy Victims

Police in Zimbabwe have identified 39 more victims of the Kariba RIDA boat tragedy. This brings the total number of positively identified victims to 83. The latest group includes 21 children, including a one-month-old baby, and 18 adults. The overall death toll has risen to 92, according to the latest police update. Identification of the remaining victims continues in cooperation with families and authorities. Police have urged relatives of people still missing after the accident to contact their nearest police station or the command centre in Kariba. Meanwhile, the government has blamed Mbuya Nehanda ferry captain Sign Patsikadova for the Kariba disaster.

South Africa Takes SADC Chair Amid Push for Regional Trade

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

South Africa has taken over the chairmanship of the Southern African Development Community (SADC) with a focus on boosting regional trade, industrialisation and infrastructure, amid concerns over weak economic growth and persistent trade barriers. SADC's latest assessment shows intra-regional trade reached 20% in 2025. Nine non-tariff barriers remain unresolved, and manufacturing's contribution to GDP fell to 10.9%, well below the bloc's 2030 target. President Cyril Ramaphosa also addressed tensions over undocumented migrants, expressing concern over discrimination against nationals from neighbouring countries. During its year-long chairmanship, South Africa plans to promote regional value chains, including processing of critical minerals and agricultural products, and strengthen the bloc's Regional Development Fund.

25 Killed in Nigeria Plateau Village Attack

At least 25 people, mostly women and children, were killed when armed men attacked the village of Bin-Per in Nigeria's Plateau State. The attackers reportedly went from house to house, killing residents with machetes, in an incident that follows a series of retaliatory attacks in the area. Local officials and community groups have accused authorities of failing to adequately protect residents as violence between mainly Christian farmers and Fulani herders continues over land and resources. Amnesty International estimated that at least 2,630 people had been killed in Plateau State between 2023 and May 2025.

Tigray Unveils First New School Curriculum in 16 Years Amid Funding Shortages

Tigray has launched a new general education curriculum after 16 years under the previous framework. It seeks to integrate indigenous knowledge and modern competency-based teaching, and to adapt to technological transformations, including artificial intelligence. However, the Tigray Education Bureau warned that funding shortages and limited textbooks could hamper implementation when the new academic year begins. The framework was developed by university scholars and education experts with $550,000 in UNICEF funding. But federal budget blockages mean only about $200,000 was said to be available. The new curriculum also introduces Ethics in primary schools, delays the introduction of Amharic to Grade 7, and expands secondary-level academic and vocational pathways. Tigray continues rebuilding an education system severely disrupted by war.

Nigerian Influencer Arrested Over Alleged Cocaine Trafficking Network

A Nigerian social media influencer known as "KC Luxury" has been arrested over alleged links to an international cocaine trafficking network. The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency said that Afolabi Kazeem Micheal, 49, was detained at Lagos airport while attempting to fly to Paris. This comes days after authorities seized 184.5kg of cocaine worth nearly $28 million at a Lagos courier facility. Investigators allege Michael was a key figure in a network moving cocaine from South America through Nigeria to Europe and Asia. A logistics company employee was also arrested. Other suspected members of the network have reportedly been detained overseas. Neither suspect has commented on the allegations or been charged in court.

World.title: South Africa: Jayden Meek Murder Trial Resumes - South African News Briefs - August 19, 2026
World.content:
Jayden Meek Murder Trial Resumes

The murder trial of Tiffany Nicole Meek, accused of killing her 11-year-old son Jayden Lee Meek, is set to resume at the Johannesburg High Court sitting at Palm Ridge Magistrates Court, reports EWN. The State is expected to call witnesses including Jayden’s school transport driver and teacher. Meek has pleaded not guilty. In the previous hearing, Sergeant Rito Koveni testified that Meek had accused the transport driver of involvement in Jayden’s disappearance. Koveni also told the court that Meek appeared unusually calm during the search, raising suspicions that she knew where her son was. The defence questioned why these suspicions were only formally recorded after Meek’s arrest.

Suspended Cop Fannie Nkosi Back in Court



Suspended police Sergeant Fannie Nkosi is expected to return to the Pretoria North Regional Court, reports SABC News. Nkosi, who was attached to the Organised Crime Unit, was suspended in March after a police task team searched his home. They allegedly found firearms, police ammunition, cash and official police dockets. He faces charges including theft, fraud and defeating the ends of justice, as well as a separate case in Limpopo involving alleged theft of marijuana from police custody. The two cases have since been consolidated. Nkosi remains in custody after his bail application was denied and a High Court appeal was dismissed.

Judgment Due in Chidimma Deportation Case

The Cape Town Regional Court is set to deliver judgment on whether Nigerian pageant queen Chidimma Adetshina should remain in detention pending possible deportation, reports EWN. Adetshina was arrested in June after allegedly entering South Africa illegally through the Lebombo border, despite being declared a prohibited person. Her identity and travel documents were cancelled in 2024 after her mother was accused of fraudulently registering her birth. Her lawyers said that Adetshina was never implicated in that fraud. They argue that an immigration agency submitted a disputed bank statement used in a visa application. Home Affairs, however, said that she re-entered South Africa in 2025 despite being on a visa-restricted list.
