World.title: Scots College denies shielding boys because parents were donors
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWEducation Scots College denies shielding boys because parents were donors Ben Cubby and Emily Kowal August 19, 2026 — 7:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Scots College has hit back against claims from parents that the prestigious private school had reacted poorly to the ongoing sexual assault scandal because the families of some of the boys who have been charged were financial donors to the school. The students – a 13-year-old boy and two 14-year-old boys – were charged with aggravated sexual assault after an alleged attack on a girl in a Bondi Junction laneway on July 22. Scots College in Bellevue Hill. The prestigious school has been accused of mishandling sexual assault allegations involving three students. Sam Mooy Some parents told the Herald they were concerned the school was downplaying the seriousness of the incident because of financial donations previously made by families of two of the three boys, who cannot be legally identified. Scots College principal Dr Ian Lambert defended the school’s “active and continuing” handling of the crisis, and said he intended to remain in his role until his planned retirement at the end of next year amid calls for his resignation.



“The suggestion that the college is shielding any student because of a family donation is false,” Lambert, who has held the title of school principal for 19 years, said in a statement. Scots College principal Dr Ian Lambert defended the school’s handling of the crisis. “Donations have no bearing whatsoever on decisions concerning student welfare, attendance or discipline. “The same standards apply to every student, with each case considered on its facts and in accordance with law, not according to family circumstances or public pressure.” One concerned parent with a student at the private boys’ school said the anger [among parents] was palpable.



Related Article Exclusive

Crime Scots College briefs boys as young as 10 on sexual assault allegations as council backs principal “The accusation is horrifying and, of course, we worry about the effect on our boy, anybody would. The students will be tarred with same brush. Honestly, I think they would have had their enrolment looked into already if they hadn’t donated,” the parent said. Another parent said the school had failed to substantially address her questions about culture in relation to the alleged assault on July 22 and previous incidents at the elite institution. “I’m appalled at how the school has responded,” said the parent with a boy in the same year group as the three boys charged with sex offences. “It’s how you react when these things happen that define you. And the way that the school is reacting right now is appalling personally as a parent, as a woman, as a human being. You don’t have to be a woman.



“It’s just not the culture I want my son in.” The question of financial donations is considered sensitive by many in the school community because Scots College is heavily dependent on cash gifts from parents, with more than 400 names listed on the school’s donations register. The school’s $60 million John Cunningham Student Centre, built in the style of a Scottish baronial castle, was in large part funded by donations. Alex Donnini On Monday, in the midst of the sexual assault scandal, the school ran its annual giving day, in which individual donations were matched by wealthy donors or corporate sponsors. For $1000, a donor would receive their name on a tile at the school’s future aquatic centre. Philanthropic giving generally yields the school about $4 million to $6 million a year, according to its financial disclosures. However, much larger sums have been obtained from the school community to fund capital works programs.



Related Article Exclusive

Private schools Text messages emerge in Scots College rape case amid calls for principal’s resignation The school’s $60 million John Cunningham Student Centre, built in the style of a Scottish baronial castle, was in large part funded by donations, including a gift of more than $12 million from Cunningham, a former student, management consultant and honorary consul general of Barbados in Australia. Three other families gave more than $1 million each towards the building’s construction, while another 81 families, trusts and foundations kicked in tens of thousands each to get the project off the ground, according to school records. The median income of households with children at the Bellevue Hill school was $336,000 in 2024, and fees can be among the highest in the nation at more than $50,000 a year. Parents and former students said they could only speak anonymously of their concerns about the school’s culture because they were worried about a backlash against their children.



Lambert said their fears were unfounded. “The college does not take disciplinary action against students because a parent or former student has lawfully expressed a concern or opinion about the college,” he said. “We expect genuine concerns to be raised directly with the college so they can be answered, while every member of our community must protect young people’s privacy and welfare and respect the legal process.” It is not the first time Lambert has been forced to defend the school against claims of sexual assault by Scots College boys. In 2021, several Sydney private schools, including Scots, faced allegations raised in an online petition – launched by former Kambala student Chanel Contos – that students had assaulted young women.



Related Article Opinion

Crime When the accused in sex crimes are children, school leaders must wake up to a toxic culture Chanel Contos Founder of Teach Us Consent Women described waking up naked at parties after passing out due to intoxication, with male peers penetrating them. Other students said they were physically forced to perform oral sex on a male while intoxicated, sometimes while the boy’s friends were present or filming the incident. Lambert said at the time: “It is a wake-up call for us all.” When asked on Wednesday whether the college would be reviewing its education around consent and behavioural expectations of students in light of the assault allegations, he said: “We do not accept that charges against individual students establish a failure of education, or that a difference between our methods and others’ preferences constitutes a deficiency.



“Consent, dignity, respectful relationships, self-control and personal responsibility are taught age-appropriately and cumulatively throughout a student’s years at Scots, grounded in Christian conviction.” With Chris Harris, Riley Walter and Natassia Chrysanthos Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. An off-the-plan apartment buyer in a huge riverfront project has criticised an “appalling” lack of communication from the developer, amid renewed questions about the project’s future. Teneriffe Banks at Skyring Terrace in Teneriffe is slated to comprise five towers with 212 apartments, a Kimpton Hotel, shops, restaurants, bars, and an extension of the riverwalk. Kokoda Property Group is behind the project, which is expected to cost about $1.5 billion. An earlier plan for Teneriffe Banks had included a skybridge linking two towers, but the feature was scrapped during a redesign. Kokoda Property Group In July it emerged that one of its entities, Riverd Pty Ltd, had gone into administration, owing more than $90 million.



The developer was adamant it would have no impact on Teneriffe Banks. After media reports suggested the administration cast a cloud over the project’s funding, Kokoda Property Group wrote to buyers on July 27 to dismiss concerns. The Teneriffe Banks site on Skyring Terrace has been cleared, but construction work was yet to begin on Wednesday. William Davis A spokesperson did not say what Riverd Pty Ltd – which had previously been called Kokoda Property Group Pty Ltd – did when contacted by this masthead on Wednesday evening, only that it was not relevant to the development. “We have obviously a great deal of entities, given that we’re a property developer and have multiple different projects,” they said.



“[Teneriffe Banks’] funding is secured … everything is tracking along really nicely.” An artist’s impression of the $1.5 billion Teneriffe Banks development. Kokoda Property Group The spokesperson added that the first stage of development remained on track for 2028, with construction to begin late this year or early 2027. A second buyer at Teneriffe Banks said they were not overly concerned by recent developments, and believed their apartment would be delivered. The Kokoda spokesperson added that the sprawling marina shown in marketing material would absolutely be built as pictured, despite questions previously being raised about its approval process. World.title: Over 100 olympic pools of ‘bin juice’ from this Perth tip is seeping into the ground
World.content:
NationalWAWaste Over 100 olympic pools of ‘bin juice’ from this Perth tip is seeping into the ground Alistair Kirkby Indigo Lemay-Conway and August 19, 2026 — 8:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There is no secret that the smell from a landfill stinks. But the real concern is what is beneath the surface. At Tamala Park Waste Facility, situated in Perth’s northern suburbs, the answer to that is leachate, and a lot of it. Tamala Park opened in 1991. Mindarie Regional Council Tamala Park landfill is run by the Mindarie Regional Council and has accepted the household waste of 800,000 Perth homes for 35 years. The council is made up of seven local governments and was due to reach the end of its operational life around 2028, however, an excessive buildup of liquid waste is now threatening to derail those closure plans.



As of October 2024, data shows there were 167 olympic sized swimming pools worth of leachate accumulated at the bottom of the tip. Without any removal methods in place, that number is expected to have risen. The situation has now triggered formal regulatory enforcement. Western Australia’s Department of Water and Environmental Regulation issued the regional council an official Environmental Protection Notice on August 3. The notice requires the MRC to provide a detailed and accurate determination of the leachate levels as well as a leachate removal plan, and they have 30 days to do it. The EPN also requires the council to improve its landfill gas management, provide updated landfill closure planning, and undertake additional technical investigations. Western Sydney University science professor Ian Wright has been a water scientist for 30 years and describes leachate as the liquid often seen at the bottom of household bins.



“Leachate is the liquid that builds up in rotting rubbish. So a lot of people might have seen it if your garbage bin with lots of food and kitchen scraps has been left in the house, and you perhaps went away for a few days,” he said. Western Sydney University science professor Ian Wright. “It’s often a tea-coloured liquid that stinks, and it’s basically decomposing waste, and it’s chemically full of lots and lots of contaminants.” Wright said the 167 olympic pools worth of leachate was a significant amount to be accumulated at the bottom of any tip and that it was “a major issue” for groundwater health. The landfill is only partially lined and the MRC’s recent request to install a piggyback liner and create a leachate management area in the northern portion of the tip – closest to the nearby residential homes – was rejected by DWER at the beginning of August.



A DWER spokesperson said the high leachate levels was one of the reasons behind the decision. “Highly elevated leachate levels were a significant consideration during the assessment of a piggyback liner and leachate management area,” they said. “Following detailed technical assessment, DWER concluded that the proposed works would generate additional leachate and would not adequately address the existing leachate, odour and groundwater issues at the site.” The regulatory body also acknowledged there are ongoing investigations into groundwater contamination at the site but that there is currently a “low” risk to human health and the broader environment. Wright said he was “very surprised” the landfill hadn’t been fully lined as to prevent groundwater contamination of the nearby Gnangara aquifer, which provides almost half of all the water used in the Perth metropolitan area each year.



“As soon as I heard about this case study, my mind went straight to: could this be in any way a threat or a risk to Perth’s groundwater? Because the Gnangara sand aquifer is right on the edge of this area,” he said. Related Article Exclusive

Waste Plans trashed: Where to dump one-third of Perth’s household waste? “It’s easy for waste from something like this landfill to move through sand down to the aquifer, so as to contaminate the groundwater.” Wright said groundwater contamination wasn’t the only risk associated with leachate buildup as methane can also be a byproduct of the breakdown of household waste. “With all this rotting landfill, and particularly the organic wastes that start breaking down, because it’s sealed under metres and metres of landfill, it starts breaking down away from oxygen, and that can create the perfect environment for methane,” he said.



Methane presents a threefold-hazard for Wright: it’s a bad greenhouse gas, it stinks, and it’s explosive. “The thing with methane is it stinks. There are suburbs growing around here, and I’m actually very surprised there isn’t a larger buffer around this landfill for the suburban development,” he said. “Methane can also blow up, and one of the concerns in the auditor’s report is that it is an explosive gas, and the gas coming from this rotting waste underground can actually rise through the surface, through the layers of soil and landfill, and if there are buildings nearby, it can sometimes rise into them. “It can even go through concrete slabs, concrete is a porous material. It can build up in buildings, and yes, it can build up to explosive levels.” Wright said he would encourage the MRC to embrace the residents and their concerns around the leachate.



“Outrage can ferment with something like this,” he said. Resident Mary O’Byrne has been championing the odour issue at Tamala Park for years and is now calling on government officials to step in. “My concern is the groundwater, what’s happening to that, and how it affects residents,” she said. “I want a government inquiry into how this place is run. I want to know why, for three and a half years, they didn’t evaporate the leachate.” Mary O’Byrne is a resident who has been campaigning against the odour and environmental concerns at Tamala Park Waste Facility. 9 News Perth



Wright said he felt like the council was trying to do their best to mitigate the problems that likely began long before most councillors were in their roles. “I can see that the council is trying their absolute best to take account of all those decisions in the past, and manage it best for locals, but there’s lots of challenges here,” he said. A spokesperson for the MRC said they were taking the management of the landfill and the protection of the surrounding environment “extremely seriously”. “Elevated levels of leachate within the landfill is an issue that both MRC and the regulator have been aware of for some time. We share DWER’s concerns on this matter and are committed to finding a viable and lasting solution,” they said. “MRC presented this information to the regulator voluntarily, and we have worked with the Department for several years to monitor and manage the site’s environmental risks and to ensure the landfill can be safely and successfully rehabilitated.”



But they said they couldn’t quantify the amount of leachate contained within the landfill and that it was a focus of their work in the coming months. “We continue to deploy measures on site to control the amount of leachate generated, to prioritise the capping of open landfill areas, and to optimise odour management.” Wright warns however that it will take many decades to manage the leachate issues on the site. “Grandchildren of people living in this area will still have to deal with this,” he said.

World.title: The ‘catastrophic failure’ that could win mushroom murderer Erin Patterson a retrial
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts The ‘catastrophic failure’ that could win mushroom murderer Erin Patterson a retrial Erin Pearson August 19, 2026 — 8:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A hotel bungle is at the centre of death cap mushroom killer Erin Patterson’s fight for freedom as her new legal team fleshes out seven reasons it says she was wrongly convicted of murdering her in-laws. The 51-year-old’s new barrister, Richard Edney, told a panel of three Court of Appeal judges in Melbourne on Wednesday that an “inexplicable failure” to separate the jury from the public, prosecution and police during deliberations created a potential miscarriage of justice. Erin Patterson watched Wednesday’s appeal hearing via video link. Anita Lester In the days after an 11-week-long trial wrapped up in Morwell in Victoria’s east in mid-2025, the court heard, jurors were sequestered for their deliberations in the same Traralgon hotel as prosecution and police involved in the case, which Edney said was a catastrophic and fundamental failure to comply with the rules. Patterson arriving at court for her sentencing hearing last August. Jason Edwards



He also raised concerns that members of the media seemed to know more about potential interactions between the jury and others at the Latrobe Valley hotel than the prosecution did, with no CCTV to ease concerns when jury keepers reported no contact had occurred with anyone outside the jury pool. It was the first time in the state’s history, he said, this was believed to have occurred. “Something has gone wrong,” Edney said. “This wasn’t the case where the only possible accommodation was this hotel.” Erin Patterson’s new legal team led by Richard Edney (centre) outside court on Wednesday. Joe Armao



Director of Public Prosecutions Brendan Kissane, KC, dismissed the claim, saying it had no substance. He said while it wasn’t ideal and was perhaps nothing more than an accident, jurors had been housed on a separate floor and ate in a separate conference room to other hotel guests. Kissane said he agreed with a July 2025 email from the trial judge that the bungle had occurred due to a shortage of accommodation in the district and that the arrangement was undesirable. “No interaction [occurred]. If something went on … we would know,” Kissane said. OPP director Brendan Kissane, KC, (right) alongside barrister Jeremy McWilliams. Joe Armao



On September 8, now retired Supreme Court judge Christopher Beale sentenced Patterson to life in prison, with a non-parole period of 33 years, after she was convicted of the murder of her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail’s sister, Heather Wilkinson. She was also convicted of the attempted murder of Baptist pastor Ian Wilkinson. The four had been fed beef Wellington laced with death cap mushrooms during a lunch at Erin Patterson’s Leongatha home in July 2023 but Ian Wilkinson survived. Simon Patterson, the killer’s estranged husband, had also been invited to the lunch but cancelled the evening before. Victims (from left) Don Patterson, Gail Patterson, Heather Wilkinson and Ian Wilkinson. In October, the DPP launched an appeal against Erin Patterson’s 33-year jail sentence, arguing it was “manifestly inadequate” for her crimes.



A month later, Patterson’s legal team filed an application to appeal her convictions and submitted there were seven reasons to quash the verdicts. These included claims that Patterson had been unfairly grilled by Crown prosecutor Nanette Rogers, SC, during eight days in the witness box, that 35 errors had occurred in Rogers’ closing address, that large amounts of evidence should not have been put before the jury, and evidence from Facebook friends and Facebook messages was not relevant. These reasons, the defence team told the court, caused Patterson a substantial miscarriage of justice. If the judges rule in her favour, Patterson could be retried. Edney labelled the hotel bungle and other issues Patterson’s legal team has with the trial as catastrophic miscarriages of justice. The defence lawyers argued that while the killer had been asked too many repetitive and improperly phrased questions, other witnesses had not been grilled enough.



The defence said Patterson had been forced to testify because of the prosecution’s submission that she had lied to police. She testified for eight days, during which she tried to explain to the jury why her story had changed. “She was compelled at that point in time. It compromised her right to silence,” junior defence barrister Veronika Drago said. On Wednesday, Ian Wilkinson arrived at the court with his two daughters, Ruth and Elizabeth, by his side. Seven members of the Patterson and Wilkinson families sat across two rows, with Wilkinson sitting in the front wooden court pew between senior homicide squad detectives Nigel L’Estrange and informant Stephen Eppingstall.



Ian Wilkinson and family members leave court on Wednesday. Eddie Jim Seated closely behind Wilkinson was Don Patterson’s brother Colin, who took scrupulous notes, as he did every day of the murder trial in Morwell last year. They appeared composed, as they were during the Morwell trial, as they listened to the defence argue that Erin Patterson had been treated unjustly. Wilkinson rested his head in his right hand at times just behind Kissane, the state’s most senior Crown prosecutor and the man tasked with ensuring Patterson stays behind bars. On Thursday, Kissane will make the case that Patterson should die in prison. Erin Patterson; a beef Wellington. Marta Pascual Juanola, supplied



If her current sentence is upheld, she will remain in jail until she is in her 80s. Documentary makers, authors and podcasters joined mainstream print and television media in the crowd of observers in Melbourne’s Supreme Court building, alongside dozens of members of the public, some of whom had travelled to Morwell to watch the original trial. Notably absent from the prosecution team on Wednesday were Nanette Rogers, SC, and junior barrister Jane Warren, who has since resigned from the OPP and is now a barrister in private practice. Patterson’s Leongatha home, the scene of the fatal lunch. Joe Armao The court heard Heather Wilkinson and Gail Patterson died on August 4, 2023, from multiple organ failure and altered liver function, with a diagnosis of amanita mushroom poisoning. Don Patterson died the following night from multiple organ failure.



Medical staff had determined the illnesses suffered by the three victims were unsurvivable, leading to their deaths from mushroom poisoning. Ian Wilkinson survived after spending several weeks in an induced coma. A court sketch of Patterson on Wednesday. Anita Lester In the end, it won’t be a country jury but three esteemed Court of Appeal judges – Stephen McLeish, Leslie Taylor and Peter Kidd – who will decide Patterson’s fate. The appeal continues on Thursday.

World.title: Sacked worker forced to pay for using ‘plain wrong’ AI in landmark case
World.content:
Exclusive BusinessWorkplaceUnfair dismissal Sacked worker forced to pay for using ‘plain wrong’ AI in landmark case Millie Muroi August 19, 2026 — 8:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A sacked Aldi store assistant who used AI to make a “just plain wrong” argument he was unfairly dismissed has been forced to pay $1230 toward the supermarket’s legal costs in the first ruling effectively punishing a former employee for wasting the Fair Work Commission’s time. On Wednesday, the country’s workplace umpire, which has highlighted the rise of nonsensical AI-generated applications that have led to an explosion in its workload and slowed down its processes, said the latest case involving AI was one with “no winner”. The Fair Work Commission said the Aldi worker’s AI-generated claim was not “complete AI slop” but that it made irrelevant arguments. Getty The case is a sharp contrast to a victory for a Macquarie University worker who used AI successfully to become the first casual employee to win orders from Fair Work last week converting him to permanent part-time status, over the opposition of the educational institution’s lawyers. Wednesday’s case shows a new potential pitfall for workers who rely on AI in making their claims in Fair Work, despite the jurisdiction originally being set up as a free forum to help employees.



Fair Work Commission deputy president Michael Easton said the Sydney Aldi worker, who had used AI extensively to start and continue his unfair dismissal claim, had ignored multiple warnings he might have to pay costs and pressed ahead with his claim when it was clear he could not win. “I have taken the very rare step of ordering [the man] to pay some of the employer’s legal costs because his unreasonable conduct caused his former employer to incur those costs unnecessarily,” Easton said. Crucially, the man was not eligible to make an unfair dismissal claim because he had not served the minimum employment period of six months. He had been dismissed on a date three days short of the minimum requirement, but his AI-generated materials had, from the beginning of the application process, focused on a “different and irrelevant date” according to the judgment. A week before the hearing was due, Easton reviewed the materials filed by both sides and decided the man’s case was “hopeless” because it failed to meet the eligibility requirements.



The initial application filed by the man was “obviously prepared using AI” Easton said, containing AI drafting notes including: “Here is your **final clean copy-paste version**, with today’s date inserted as the dismissal date.” Related Article Unfair dismissal Employee sacked for failing to return to office despite contract allowing WFH “I took the time to write to [the man] and explain to him well ahead of the hearing, in plain English, why his case was unlikely to succeed,” Easton said. “[He] was encouraged to discontinue his application, and advised that there could be costs consequences if he continues his claim.” The man’s AI-generated email reply once again addressed the wrong end date, Easton said, and repeated the same irrelevant AI-generated arguments. “I took further time to send [the man] another email in the hope everybody’s time and costs would not be wasted by attending a hearing,” Easton said, stating in “much stronger terms” the “very strong likelihood” that his case would not win and that he would have to pay Aldi’s costs, after it applied for compensation.



The man continued his case and sent two further AI-generated submissions that again addressed the wrong end date, Easton said. It was not until the hearing, where Easton raised the same concerns, that the man, for the first time, agreed that he had not completed the minimum employment period and decided to discontinue his application. However, the man tried to argue he could not reasonably have been expected to understand the distinction between the date he was notified of his dismissal and the date the dismissal took effect because he “is not a legal expert.” Easton said the man’s submission was “not complete AI slop, as that term has come to be used,” in that some of the legal arguments presented were “more or less correct, though irrelevant”, and the High Court cases cited were real cases rather than hallucinations. However, he said the submission still focused on the effective date of the man’s dismissal, which was labelled as being “unresolved” despite there being “no doubt” about it.



The man was ordered to pay $1230 in legal costs Aldi wasted in preparing for and attending a hearing that, according to Easton, “should never have taken place” with losses for both parties that were “utterly preventable”. That represented a small part of Aldi’s overall costs, Easton noted. Easton said that had the man read the emails from the commission himself, he would have realised the “unfixable flaw” in his case. “[The man] could have and should have chosen to cut his losses when he had the chance,” Easton concluded. Aldi was contacted for comment. Get workplace news, advice and perspectives to help make your job work for you.

World.title: What Brisbane can learn from the Germans about bike lights
World.content:
Perspective NationalQueenslandCycling What Brisbane can learn from the Germans about bike lights Tom Joyce August 19, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In these fractious times, at least we can all agree on one thing: how much nicer it was when bicycles were slow and merely annoying. Back when bikes were propelled by honest toil: Wear that helmet, ring that bell, run that red, and there’ll be hell. Then came the zeal of putting electricity into places it was never meant to go. We woke up one morning to discover that marauding youths on e-bikes had taken over the Story Bridge and were upending rubbish bins. Their reign of terror is finally being regulated, but just as we tamed the Frankenbike, a new menace rolled into view. Extremely bright lights on the Bicentennial Bikeway along the river. Tom Joyce After a night ride that took in the Coronation Drive bikeway, I arrived home dazed and convinced that I’d suffered retinal bleaching. Unhelpfully, a medical friend downgraded it to “intraocular scatter”, which sounded tone-deaf to my suffering. So retinal bleaching it is.



Count me gullible, but I thought the defanging of e-bikes would allow decent folk – people like us – to reclaim our streets. I was wrong. Related Article Exclusive

City life One-way traffic and 40km/h limits planned for notorious Toowong black spot Meet the all-singing, all-blinding matrix LED bicycle lights that have retina-melting outputs beyond that of a car and sell online for less than the price of a KFC family bucket. Attached to a bicycle handlebar, they give the impression that Suncorp Stadium, lights ablaze, has somehow come loose and is pedalling straight towards you. How did commuter bikes end up with special-forces lighting? Technology, culture and – because they’re bicycles – a regulatory ho-hum and a shrug. Some blame the Americans, which seems to fit the moment. Others say we should have copied the Germans, which rarely fits the moment. Instead, we followed the Brits, and so we did almost nothing. Bike‑light rules are set by Queensland and the other states, but they’re all based on the same federal template that’s barely been updated since the 1960s.



In the same way that bicycles were largely tame and overlooked until batteries and electric motors turned them into monsters, the retinal searing that is now the nightly curse throughout the land came upon us slowly … and then very quickly indeed. We don’t permit car drivers to get about on their high beam blinding oncoming drivers. The logic is clear enough – it’s blinding, and therefore unsafe. Attached to a handlebar, they give the impression that Suncorp Stadium, lights ablaze, has come loose and is pedalling straight towards you. Pedalling at 25km/h, even mild glare wipes out seven metres of vision, while strong glare gives you a milky haze and a cricket pitch of blindness. And all this in the pursuit of “better lighting”. The Americans invented night mountain biking in the 1970s and needed lights bright enough to turn entire forests into daylight. Their $400 halogen rigs trickled into commuting.



Not having ridden at night for a few years, I didn’t realise that welding goggles were essential for after-dark eye protection. Coming towards me was a conga line of tactical lights, the kind probably sold under categories like “Optical Suppression” and “Visual Acuity Denial”. The first blinding light seemed brighter and more disconcerting than any errant car high-beam I’d ever faced, so no surprise to learn that 20 bucks from Temu will arm you with enough visual acuity denial to blind a Roman legion, should you encounter one, or twice the lumens of a car headlamp and none of the optics. On a typical weeknight, the problem exists all along the river. Tom Joyce Filled with recent knowledge of how regulators had seemingly put the pedal back in velocipedes, I thought I must be missing something. Had technology snuck up again and flipped the world on its head?



Australia slavishly followed the UK’s 1960s bike-light rules; a minimalist white front, red rear, visible from 200 yards. No beam pattern, no cut-off, no glare control. Related Article City life One week into e-bike crackdown, 63 bikes and scooters seized America treated bike lights as tactical gear and worshipped lumens, even if it meant bathing every other road user in your light. Now meet the Germans – the sensible guys in the room. Straßenverkehrs‑Zulassungs‑Ordnung looks like something you might see on an unrented roadside billboard, followed up with “There, made you look”.



Better known as StVZO, it’s the Germans’ road traffic code, and it simply treats bicycles as vehicles. That means bike lights must have proper optics: cut-off beams, glare limits, light measured by what illuminates the road, not strangers’ corneas. Related Article City life ‘Are you out of your mind?’: Near-crash between scooter and toddler divides opinion Most of the “2000 lumens” people are so proud of is literally being fired into the sky, hedges and other people’s retinas, not the road ahead. Our regulatory stutter and splutter when high-powered e-bikes appeared should have taught us something. But we’re now awash in the blinding glare of unregulated stadium lights that blind cyclists nightly. Keen for another night-time bike ride, I’ve gone on Temu and bought a full-face welder’s helmet – $21.30. I may not be able to see the road ahead at night – which some would say comes with its own hazards – but no more will I be retinally bleached.



It’ll have to do until retinal bleaching and visual acuity denial are consigned to the Frankenbike scrapheap as well. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: AFL needs to use its power to effect change
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters AFL needs to use its power to effect change August 19, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Columnist Angela Pippos (Comment, 19/8) makes the point that men in football have the power to create a safer and fairer environment for women, if the will is there. My son is a 20-year veteran of the game. He says that this is an opportunity for the AFL to come out and insist on meaningful change at every level of the game. The AFL has spent years telling us about the power of football to influence society. Well, here’s an opportunity to prove it. Not with another glossy campaign, another carefully crafted statement or another round of lip service, but by actually demanding better behaviour and accountability across the entire football culture. Talk needs to become action – respect women, challenge misogyny and don’t stand by when behaviour crosses the line. The AFL has enormous influence. It also has an enormous opportunity. The question is whether it intends to use that influence to actually change football culture, or simply wait until the next scandal comes along and release another statement.

Carolyn Brydon, Brighton East Stand up against men’s behaviour

Angela Pippos calls it out. Men’s misogynistic behaviour is not just confined to the football world, it’s everywhere. Stand up for your sisters when you see and read it. Pippos got that right. But standing up to it is always right.

Margaret Skeen, Ocean Grove Language matters in these times

Past and present AFL leaders, current and former players and media ″⁣personalities″⁣ continue to make excuses for the inexcusable behaviour of their own. They fail to ″⁣read the room″⁣ on how broader society views their appalling attitudes and dismissiveness towards women. Thank you to Angela Pippos in explaining that language matters. Players are adults, and surely in charge of their own destinies – if they are unable to manage their behaviour off the ground then should they be permitted on the ground?

Felicity Browne, Toorak



Male-dominated culture has lot to answer for

I am appalled at the reaction and some of the media reporting surrounding the recent sexual assault allegations. The very first reaction was not compassion for the alleged female victim, it was how this would affect the players and an AFL club and competition so close to the finals. Where on earth have our priorities gone, in this whole atrocious event? This male-dominated sporting culture sure has a lot to answer for.

Frank Flynn, Cape Paterson The women must not be forgotten

Although we do not know the full details of the alleged sexual assault, I am sure there are many stories circulating in the community. The focus of the news reports have been on the timing of the incident at the pointy end of the season, and how the players have let down their team and their partners. Because this is a police matter the details of the incident have not been divulged, but the hyperbole is out of control. What about respect for the women involved, not only in the incident but in general as women are often painted not as victims but as seducers? There is no place for sexual misconduct in our society, and the boys will be boys attitude is not good enough.

Julie Ottobre, Brunswick East ‘Shocked and disappointed’ at CEO message

Thank you for The Age editorial, and column from Angela Pippos (19/8) specifically highlighting the passive language used by Sydney Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich. Given his leadership position, I was ″⁣shocked and disappointed” that he implied the players involved had somehow just fallen into the situation. Pippos’s article debunks this. Just imagine if a man had taken the leadership and time to put out such a clear message.

Sally Polmear, Barkers Creek THE FORUM NDIS ripple effects

My 36-year-old intellectually disabled daughter cannot take herself to the movies. She cannot even cross the road by herself. The NDIS promised reasonable and necessary services to maintain as near a normal lifestyle, with dignity, opportunity and access to social and community experiences, as the rest of us. Now the NDIS changes seeks to slash by half or more anything that comes into that orbit.

My daughter reasonably and necessarily requires the assistance of a support worker to take her out of the house she shares with and in which she is cared for by oldish parents, say once a week. This is to do ordinary things like walking or being driven to the shops, the park, beach, a gallery, show, movie, meeting friends, having a coffee, walking a dog or whatever. The NDIS only pays for the worker’s hours no matter what the activity or location of the care undertaken and the rate is the same as in-home care. All expenses like movie tickets are covered by my daughter as has always been the case despite wild exaggerations about what NDIS actually pays for and who is rorting the system. Her plan has always been strictly monitored and is in keeping with pre-NDIS days to maintain her wellbeing, safety and security.

Are people like her now to be confined to their rooms or in front of a TV or video with little opportunity to join in and enjoy the life of Melbourne and suburbs like any other 36-year-old?

Kaye Powell, Malvern



Opt-out is useless

The gambling legislation, supported by the Coalition, looks like it will be passed with an “opt-out ability”. This is likely to be as ineffective as the “do not call register”, which was useless. It will only apply to online advertising. We, and our children, will still be subjected to all other types of advertising on TV, radio, and all printed forms of advertising.

Monique Ryan hit the nail in the head with her speech in parliament opposing this legislation when she said Anthony Albanese was not listening to the people who overwhelmingly support the banning of gambling advertising.

Jenny Callaghan, Hawthorn Gambling a health issue

The government has sidestepped taking strong action to curb gambling (″⁣Gambling can police itself? Good luck with that notion″⁣, 19/8). This is despite the recommendations of the Murphy inquiry, input from the Greens, churches and welfare groups, many of whom deal with the harmful effects of gambling.

The main reason for the government’s reluctance to act on gambling reform is that it generates a huge amount of tax revenue – about $10 billion for all states. Electronic gambling machines are the largest cash generators for the government. In the Northern Territory, 12.1 per cent of its total revenue comes from gambling. As well as this, gambling is an integral part of the Australia social system and Australians are now the biggest gamblers in the world and also the world’s biggest losers per capita. But the adverse effects of gambling are destructive. Nearly two-thirds in every dollar going into a poker machine come from people who are addicted to gambling.

There is an approach for gambling reform. Advocates such as Tim Costello, chief advocate at the Alliance for Gambling Reform, recommend gambling be treated like smoking – that is, as a health issue.

Australia banned smoking s in 1992 and today Australia has one of the lowest rates of smoking in the world. Tackling our gambling issue must be a priority.

Leigh Ackland, Deepdene Blind government

Once again the Albanese government demonstrates it has lost sight of the light on the hill.

Gambling is a public health issue. The social impacts are well-documented. Suicide, family violence and financial destitution are just some of the fallout from this insidious activity, the proceeds of which are largely repatriated tax free.

The impact on advertising companies and the gambling industry should never be made a consideration in the outcome of this legislation. It is appalling, although not unexpected, that the unambiguous findings of the late Peta Murphy’s report, You win some, you lose more, be treated in this contemptuous manner.

It’s a slogan that may well come to haunt Labor’s gamble on this pressing issue electorally.

John Mosig, Kew Vested interests win

Rob Harris’s concluding line “The real loser is the rest of us” best sums up the outcome of the revised gambling legislation (Analysis, 19/8).

Despite the significant community outrage at the predatory and unscrupulous behaviour of the gambling industry, laid bare yet again at the recent Senate hearings, the government and Coalition have negotiated a bill that falls well short.

Vested interests appear to have won the day over the wellbeing of our citizens. Shame on the Albanese government and the Coalition.

Anne Lyon, Camberwell Rise of the algorithm

Monday’s 4 Corners exposed algorithms rationing aged care funding, leaving almost 154,000 people waiting for support they’ve been assessed as needing, signalling a betrayal of everything the royal commission promised.

This isn’t just an aged care failure. It’s an integrity failure, and the same pattern runs through Australian life.

On climate, fossil fuel companies donated nearly $4million to the major parties last election and receive roughly $10 billion a year in subsidies, while home insurance in disaster-prone areas has risen up to 400 per cent.

In aged care, costs have outpaced funding for decades, and still the government has handed $1.5 billion in assessment contracts to for-profit providers; this is the exact conflict the royal commission warned against.

On gambling, Australians have lost over $100 billion since mid-2023, while reform decided this week does not meet the pub test.

On social media, engagement-driven algorithms feed boys a diet of misogynistic content.

Different portfolios, one pattern: vested interests get a seat at the table; Australians get the algorithm, the waitlist, and the bill.

Fix the integrity, and the rest follows.

Melissa Lowe, Hawthorn



Trump’s winning ways

The scary thing about Donald Trump’s threat to bomb Oman, an ally of the US in the Middle East, is that he won’t lose a single vote from his base who seem wedded to his ″⁣strongman″⁣ tactics. Such war-like, bullying behaviour should make him completely unelectable. Fifth Avenue, Oman; Trump gets away with it.

Nick Toovey, Beaumaris Land access for all

It goes against good rules of community wellbeing for a wealthy landowner to lease community parkland (“Community anger over bayside private school’s plan to ‘lock public out’ of park”, 19/8). Brighton Grammar claims it would thereby enhance the land, Wilson Reserve, and promises all sorts of inducements. The school also wishes to buy a public road, Young Street. The school is seeking exclusive access to the adjacent Wilson Reserve for large parts of each day, in the Brighton area which already has insufficient public space.

A better proposal would be for Brighton Grammar to allow community access to its grounds on the weekends for the community to play sport. After all, the public, via its taxes, is contributing significantly to all private schools, while public schools languish. Active and passive recreation is very important to health, so let’s even up access.

Jan Marshall, Brighton Benefits of taxes

The last party I will vote for is the party who will offer to lower taxes. I like what my taxes pay for, such as social welfare, health, education (although more should go to government schools rather than private), infrastructure, medical/scientific/environmental research, helping devastated communities here and abroad, even defence.

Why would a civil and functioning society want lower taxes?

Unless you want to live in America, which currently cannot be described as either civil or functioning.

Robyn Westwood, Heidelberg Heights Just got on with it

I am also a daughter of a Japanese POW (Letters, 19/8). My father was a POW in Japan for 3 years, having been captured in Java and spending time in Changi. Yes, he had huge issues of PTSD for his entire life, but he came home and just got on with it, as did his lifelong friend in the same situation.

They were told by the army that no one knew how their captivity would affect them, so they should just go out and live, no counselling or other support.

But my father and his friend and others who he met regularly at POW reunions never resorted to the appalling behaviour we see now.

Louise Kloot, Doncaster Just a blunt stick

One Nation is a party of protest – not progress.

The only thing they offer voters is a blunt stick to poke in the eye of the established parties. They have no defined policies for health, welfare, education or the economy, but rather an anachronistic anti-immigration policy more suited to a xenophobic white Australia from last century. Their leadership is well past its use-by dates.

Peter Ozard, Hampton



Bard weather is brewing

Regarding Shakespearean news reports (Letters, 19/8), Melbourne weather forecasts could sign off with: “To be, or not to be, that is the question.“

Deborah Morrison, Malvern East Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Gambling

Labor and the Coalition agree gambling can ″⁣police itself″⁣. Don’t bet on it (″⁣Betting bill will pass but Labor faces fresh battles″⁣, 19/8).

Annie Wilson, Inverloch The shamefully weak gambling legislation demonstrates that the biggest addicts are governments addicted to gambling taxes.

Michael Meszaros, Alphington



″⁣Squibbing it″⁣ is an apt description for the likely outcome of the gambling legislation process.

Jim Spithill, Glen Waverley Labor can ″⁣spin″⁣ their gambling reform however they like, but they’ve still welched on a true opportunity to advocate for those less able to themselves.

David Cayzer, Clifton Hill Swans

As a Swans supporter I am reminded that respect is gained in teaspoons and lost in buckets.

Stephen Dinham, Metung Whether they assaulted women or not, why did Swans players stay out drinking until early morning? Culture counts.

Glenda Johnston, Queenscliff Furthermore

4 Corners on Monday showed that the federal Public Service delivers frank and fearless advice through secret algorithms.

George Reed, Wheelers Hill



Will Anthony Albanese ensure aged people will not live in fear of insensitive algorithms?

Ralph Tabor, Pakenham If a lawn bowls club closes, it removes the ability of an aged bowler to feel young again (″⁣Brighton Bowls Club faces demolition″⁣, 18/8).

Malcolm McDonald, Burwood Donald Trump threatens to bomb ally Oman if it “gets in the way” of reopening Hormuz Strait. I suspect that both enemy and ally are finding Trump’s threats wearing thin.

Kevin Burke, Sandringham Finally

It used to be a pleasure to go for a drive in the countryside. That is no longer the case due to the potholes.

Tony O’Brien, South Melbourne

World.title: The Swans abandoned the old-school script. What happens next will shape the club’s future
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 The Swans abandoned the old-school script. What happens next will shape the club’s future Jake Niall August 19, 2026 — 7:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Once the Sydney Swans recognised that there was far more at stake than the team they would field in the 2026 finals series, the decision to ban five key players for the remainder of the season became logical. The Swans’ hierarchy made a principled decision, and their chairman Andrew Pridham and his chief executive Matthew Pavlich must be commended for that stance. Loading They read the play. The AFL was not going to tolerate anything less than a significant penalty, but the Swans did not need to be hectored, or pushed by headquarters. They arrived at that destination, themselves. They could not address matters that involved the police and, from what this column gathered, they intentionally did not question the five on the specifics of what happened in the hotel room that prompted the sexual assault allegation and police investigation.



The focus was on the events and prior behaviour (said to be in breach of club standards) that led to that investigation. They knew that the damage from those events was awful – to the reputation of club, the individual players and, regarding the later incident subject to the investigation, allegedly to the women concerned. Sydney Swans players (from left to right) Chad Warner, James Jordon, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey. Artwork: Michael Howard One could argue that if the ban reached three matches, then they might as well suspend the five for the entire season. The Swans will be long odds to beat the Brisbane Lions or Hawthorn in the qualifying final without Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey. James Jordon and Riley Bice’s absences won’t help either. It will be challenging to win a subsequent semi-final without the players, too.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Deeply sorry to everyone involved’: Suspended Swans speak out for first time But the goal of winning finals and striving to win the premiership was relegated – rightly. Pridham’s comment that they had been willing to torpedo the season encapsulated their mindset. The Swans are the flagship club of the northern states for the AFL and for the code. They are on the frontline against a revived NRL in the game’s most challenging market. Successful in their missionary mission, the Swans have profited from the perception that they are well-managed and that their players embrace a culture of diligence and decency. But AFL teams in Sydney are not subjected to the obsessive scrutiny – especially on social media now – that accompanies players from Carlton, Collingwood, Richmond et al. This anonymity is part of their appeal to quality players.



It is a more relaxed environment in which players can go for a drink without being filmed on smartphones or stalked. It is reasonable to ask whether this lack of scrutiny permits players liberties that aren’t afforded in Melbourne. No AFL club is inherently more virtuous than the others. Further, organisations’ cultures should be judged on the reaction to a stuff up, rather than merely the mistake itself. Coach Dean Cox and captain Callum Mills arrive at Swans training. George Chan Dean Cox would know how his former club, West Coast, fell into severe disrepute in the mid to late 2000s when they had a drug problem within the playing group and Ben Cousins was the poster child of an implosion. He would know that the real life consequences outweigh any on-field success. West Coast accepted that they needed to repair a broken culture and were willing to tumble down the ladder to achieve it.



Sydney’s situation is not as drastic as West Coast’s, and will not require an intervention or collateral crash on that scale. Yet, the Swans are bound to ask themselves and to probe whether this incident was a) a one-off stupidity, or b) a canary in the mine showing that their playing culture isn’t so flash. Removing the question of alleged criminal matters, the alleged presence of two women in the hotel room for the entertainment of five players sounded like the most degraded versions of end of season footy trips - brought forward to the eve of finals. For the five, it turned out to be their end of season footy trip. The unprofessionalism (as found by the club) is staggering, especially considering three are senior players on hefty contracts, not 20-year-olds.



Heeney’s fall is precipitous. He is the face of the club, wholesome and hitherto highly saleable to sponsors. Obviously, he cannot continue as member of the leadership group, which is the least of his concerns given he is the focus of the police investigation. The players have denied wrongdoing, according to a source familiar with the players’ position. It is notable that the Sydney hierarchy did not rule out offloading some of the five. Isaac Heeney in action for the Swans. Getty Images Chad Warner is a free agent next year and has the option of heading back to Perth; the prospect of joining the Eagles or Dockers may be more enticing today than on Sunday afternoon. So much is yet to play out. The expedient, well-trod path would be to jettison one or two of the lesser players, Bice and/or Jordon, to make a statement to the rest of the playing group while keeping the stars.

World.title: Tenants caught in crosshairs of angry rent-hike debate
World.content:
PoliticsFederalRenting Tenants caught in crosshairs of angry rent-hike debate Shane Wright August 19, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian renters are being warned they will be caught between US President Donald Trump’s soaring budget deficits, vested property interests and the federal government’s own changes to property taxes with the only relief likely to come from a large increase in new homes. As new figures showed a small recovery in after-inflation wages for workers, the federal government fended off accusations its overhaul of negative gearing and capital gains tax concessions will lead to the largest increases in rents ever recorded. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese during Question Time in the House of Representatives at Parliament House in Canberra. Dominic Lorrimer Critics of the budget changes, which restrict negative gearing to people with existing properties and those who build new homes while also returning the capital gains tax system to its pre-1999 link to inflation, have ramped up claims they will both crash house prices and drive up rents. Increases in rent, as measured by the Australian Bureau of Statistics, peaked in mid-2024 with the largest jumps recorded in Perth at more than 10 per cent. There were also sizeable lifts in Sydney (8.7 per cent) and Melbourne (6.8 per cent) while Brisbane’s peak of 9.8 per cent was recorded in mid-2023.



Since then, every capital city has recorded a slowdown in rent growth, but they remain high by historical standards. Over the past 12 months, rents have lifted by 5.3 per cent in Perth, by 3.5 per cent in Sydney and by 2.6 per cent in Melbourne. Independent economist Chris Richardson said by the government’s own figures, it was difficult to accept that the negative gearing changes, expected to raise $2 billion in extra revenue over four years, would cause upheaval to a property market worth $12.8 trillion. He said bigger factors were the run-up in government debt, led by the United States where gross debt will later this month surpass $US40 trillion, fuelling an increase in government interest rates. The interest rate on US debt is at its highest level in two decades and climbing. Some investors faced with a risk-free 5 per cent return on government debt compared to lower rates on rental properties may exit the market.



“As a renter I wouldn’t be greatly stressed because of what’s going on because of the tax changes, but they are on the wrong side of a whole lot of things going on right now,” he said. Fellow independent economist and long-time critic of negative gearing, Saul Eslake, said the laws of supply and demand still applied to the property market, even with the government’s tax changes. Related Article Analysis

Property market Saying there’s an upside to falling house prices is sacrilege. But Labor needs to admit it He described some of the claims about the reforms as “bullshit”, accusing “vested interests” of trying to scare renters who were now in a better position to buy their first home because of the reduced interest of investors in existing properties. “There are people who think the government should always underwrite the market to keep house prices going up,” he said.



“The share of investors buying existing homes had been growing, but now that is turning around, but the government seems unwilling to claim credit for what is happening.” Eslake likened the current debate to the furore that accompanied the Hawke government’s abolition of negative gearing between 1985 and 1987. Opponents at the time claimed the move pushed up rents across the country, forcing the government to abandon its changes. But the only markets to experience an increase in rental inflation were Sydney, where the vacancy rate was under 1 per cent, and Perth, where the vacancy rate was under 2 per cent. Rental growth actually slowed in other key markets, led by Melbourne and Brisbane. Housing Minister Clare O’Neil, who faced a string of questions in parliament over the state of the rental market, accused the Coalition of uttering “mistruths” over the state of property across the country. But she noted rent rises had slowed since the federal budget, arguing the government’s changes actually protected existing landlords while encouraging prospective investors to build new homes.



“In many respects, renters are the ones in our country who are bearing the brunt of 40 years of Australian governments not doing enough about housing. That is why our government is stepping up with the boldest agenda since the Second World War,” she said. Greens leader Larissa Waters accused real estate agents of advising “rich property investors” to hike up rents as much as possible. She said the government should deliver an immediate nationwide rent freeze. Separate figures from the Bureau of Statistics released on Wednesday showed wages grew faster than inflation over the past three months, but since June last year they have gone backwards in real terms. The wage price index increased by 0.8 per cent in the three months to June. Over the same period, inflation actually fell by 0.4 per cent.



But over the past 12 months, wages grew by 3.2 per cent – their slowest rate since 2022 – while inflation lifted by 3.8 per cent. The situation is worse for workers in the private sector, with wages up by 0.7 per cent in the quarter and by 3.1 per cent over the full year. Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson said the figures showed that real wages had fallen by $1600 a year over the life of the government, accusing it of fuelling inflation that was eating into workers’ take-home pay. “Every time the government makes a decision, they’re stoking inflation and they’re continuing to put more pressure on Australian households. Wages are going backwards, and Australians are becoming poorer,” he said. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Winter illnesses harming students' education, NZPF president says
World.content:
The principal of a Napier kura says more than half of their students are not at school this week because they are sick.

Maraenui Bilingual School Tumuaki, Traci Liddall, said 67 percent of their 125 students stayed home on Monday, and 56 percent did on Tuesday and Wednesday. All but two of those students were reported to have flu-like symptoms.

Data from the Ministry of Education showed almost 10 percent of class time was lost across the country last week due to illness. The past couple of weeks have been the worst in three years for school absences due to illness and medical reasons.

Hawke's Bay has been hit hard - one day last week, Napier Girl's High had 20 percent of its students, or about 200 girls, off due to sickness. The Terrace School - a primary in Waikpukurau - had 76 kids off on Tuesday, about a third of its roll, as well as six teachers.

Liddall said the Ministry of Education advising parents to send children to school with mild symptoms like a runny nose was unhelpful.

"It bothers me that the ministry are on our back about attendance, but we can't help this.

"As much as we would like the tamariki to be at kura, I'd rather sick kids stay at home and get properly well before they come to school, otherwise they just spread germs.

"Sending kids with sniffles is not a good message to be sending, so I'm disappointed to see that."

She said three teachers at the bilingual school, including herself, were also sick.

They had merged some classes, but they often did that due to small class numbers, to give teachers relief time.

Liddal said she had not seen sickness-related absences this high in her 30-year teaching career, other than during Covid-19.

"Fifteen to 20 percent would be a bad day for absences for us, unless there's something going on in the community, like a big tangi.

"I've never seen anything like this."

Winter illnesses are harming students' education, the president of the New Zealand Principals' Federation says.

Have you been affected by school sickness? Get in touch at iwitness@rnz.co.nz

NZPF president Jason Miles said absences that high affected student learning.

"You've got to work out what the children have missed in that time that they've been away. It's about the teachers knowing their children, knowing what they have missed and looking at what they can do to catch up," he told RNZ.

The principal's federation encouraged children to stay away if they were unwell, but to come back as soon as they were feeling better, he said.

"There are different communities that are hit harder than others for a period of time, and it takes 5-10 days to get over this flu, so in that time you've got a number of children who are sick, a number of children who about to get sick and of course you've got staff who are sick as well."

Illness among staff was particularly problematic, and was putting huge pressure on the relieving teacher pool, particularly in high schools.

"When you've got a lot of children away, it's fairly straightforward, but if you've got more staff away, percentage-wise, than children, then that's a really difficult space for leaders to be in, because that's about getting enough adults to keep your school open.

"So school leaders are either having to double up classes, put management staff in classes, which impacts on other parts of running the school, or rostering some years home."

The Ministry of Education said it shared guidance published by Health New Zealand on its website to support parents in deciding whether their child was well enough to attend school.

"We know parents are often making these decisions first thing in the morning, and it isn't always clear-cut," group general manager Helen Hurst said.

"When symptoms are mild, it may not always be obvious whether a child needs to stay home. The guidance helps parents make that call.

"Regular attendance is important for learning, but children who are sick should stay home. When they are well enough to learn, they should be at school."

Auckland Primary Principals' Association executive Lucy Naylor told the NZ Herald that parents could not afford to have a "she'll be right attitude" towards illness.

She acknowledged there could be "conflicting messaging" over when to keep children home, however.

Health NZ has official guidance for when children should not be at school.

It states: "If a child is too unwell to learn or they have an infectious illness that could spread easily to others, they need to be kept at home away from school so they can recover or get health advice or care."
